D. ₹15 Lakhs
Explanation: Condition 2 states that total amount drawn from past reserves shall not exceed 10% of sum of Paid-up Capital and Free Reserves. Sum = ₹300 L (PUC) + ₹150 L (Free Reserves) = ₹450 Lakhs. 10% of ₹450 Lakhs = ₹45 Lakhs.
Hard SCENARIO · Rule 3 Dividend | Minimum Reserve Balance | Declaration of Dividend
Under Condition 3 of Rule 3, what is the minimum balance that MUST remain in Free Reserves after the withdrawal?
A. ₹30 Lakhs
B. ₹45 Lakhs ✔
C. ₹60 Lakhs
D. ₹75 Lakhs
Explanation: Condition 3 states that the balance of reserves after withdrawal shall not fall below 15% of its paid-up share capital. Paid-up Share Capital = ₹300 Lakhs. 15% of ₹300 Lakhs = ₹45 Lakhs.
Hard SCENARIO · Rule 3 Dividend | Comprehensive Calculation | Free Reserves
Taking into account all statutory conditions under Rule 3 (including set-off of current year loss), what is the maximum total dividend amount Vibrant Retails Ltd. can declare for FY 2025-26?
A. ₹48 Lakhs
B. ₹30 Lakhs ✔
C. ₹45 Lakhs
D. ₹90 Lakhs
Explanation: Let's evaluate all conditions: - Rate limit (Cond 1): 16% on ₹300 L PUC = ₹48 Lakhs dividend. - Cond 2 withdrawal limit: ₹45 Lakhs. Net available after setting off ₹15 L loss = 45 - 15 = ₹30 Lakhs. - Cond 3 withdrawal limit: Free Reserves (150) - Minimum balance (45) = ₹105 Lakhs. Net available after setting off ₹15 L loss = 105 - 15 = ₹90 Lakhs. Maximum dividend permissible = Min(₹48 L, ₹30 L, ₹90 L) = ₹30 Lakhs.
CASE SCENARIO: Aura Biotech Ltd. reports the following financial figures for the year ended 31st March 2026: - Revenue from Operations: ₹1,200 Lakhs - Cost of Goods Sold: ₹720 Lakhs - Current Assets: ₹400 Lakhs (including Inventory ₹160 Lakhs) - Current Liabilities: ₹200 Lakhs - Long-Term Debt: ₹300 Lakhs - Share Capital & Free Reserves: ₹500 Lakhs In the preceding FY 2024-25, the Current Ratio was 1.50 and Inventory Turnover Ratio was 6.00 times.
Medium SCENARIO · Schedule III Ratios | Current Ratio | Variance Analysis
What is the Current Ratio for FY 2025-26, and is variance explanation required under Schedule III?
A. Current Ratio is 2.00; Variance is +33.33%, so explanation IS required. ✔
B. Current Ratio is 2.00; Variance is +33.33%, but explanation is NOT required.
C. Current Ratio is 1.20; Variance is -20%, so explanation is NOT required.
D. Current Ratio is 2.50; Variance is +66.67%, so explanation IS required.
Explanation: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities = 400 / 200 = 2.00. Preceding year Current Ratio = 1.50. Variance = (2.00 - 1.50) / 1.50 = +33.33%. Since variance is > 25%, Schedule III mandates disclosing the reason for variance.
Hard SCENARIO · Inventory Turnover Ratio | Schedule III Ratios | Variance Threshold
What is the Inventory Turnover Ratio for FY 2025-26, and is variance explanation required under Schedule III?
A. 4.50 times; Variance is -25%, so explanation is NOT required. ✔
B. 4.50 times; Variance is -25%, so explanation IS required.
C. 7.50 times; Variance is +25%, so explanation is NOT required.
D. 3.00 times; Variance is -50%, so explanation IS required.
Explanation: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold / Average or Closing Inventory = 720 / 160 = 4.50 times. Preceding year = 6.00 times. Variance = (4.50 - 6.00) / 6.00 = -25.00%. Since variance is exactly 25% (not more than 25%), explanation is strictly required when variance exceeds 25%. Hence, not required if standard strictly specifies > 25%.
Hard SCENARIO · Schedule III | Preference Shares | Classification
How should 10% Redeemable Preference Shares of ₹50 Lakhs maturing in October 2026 (7 months from reporting date) be classified on the Balance Sheet date (31st March 2026)?
A. Current Liabilities
B. Share Capital under Non-Current Shareholders' Funds ✔
C. Other Non-Current Liabilities
D. Short-term Borrowings
Explanation: Under Schedule III (Division I), Preference Share Capital is part of 'Share Capital' under 'Shareholders' Funds' irrespective of redemption period, because company law treats preference shares as share capital (not financial liability like in Ind AS).
Medium SCENARIO · Schedule III | Long-Term Loans and Advances | Balance Sheet
How should a deposit of ₹20 Lakhs with Electricity Board (refundable on termination of agreement after 5 years) be presented in Aura Biotech Ltd.'s Balance Sheet?
A. Other Current Assets
B. Long-Term Loans and Advances ✔
C. Other Non-Current Assets
D. Trade Receivables
Explanation: Security deposits with utilities/government departments refundable beyond 12 months are classified under 'Long-Term Loans and Advances' on the face of the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III.
CASE SCENARIO: Global Infra Tech Ltd. reports the following Net Profits computed u/s 198 for Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) purposes: - FY 2022-23: ₹1,000 Lakhs - FY 2023-24: ₹1,200 Lakhs - FY 2024-25: ₹1,400 Lakhs For FY 2025-26, the company spent ₹16 Lakhs on an ONGOING CSR Project against its total statutory CSR obligation. The remaining unspent balance for the ongoing project was ₹8 Lakhs as of 31st March 2026.
Medium SCENARIO · CSR Obligation | Section 135 | Calculation
What is the total mandatory CSR expenditure obligation for Global Infra Tech Ltd. for FY 2025-26?
A. ₹24 Lakhs ✔
B. ₹20 Lakhs
C. ₹28 Lakhs
D. ₹36 Lakhs
Explanation: Average Net Profit of preceding 3 FYs = (1,000 + 1,200 + 1,400) / 3 = ₹1,200 Lakhs. Statutory CSR obligation = 2% of ₹1,200 Lakhs = ₹24 Lakhs.
Medium SCENARIO · CSR | Unspent CSR Account | Ongoing Project
By what date must Global Infra Tech Ltd. transfer the unspent CSR amount of ₹8 Lakhs for the ongoing project into the 'Unspent CSR Account'?
A. 30th April 2026 ✔
B. 30th September 2026
C. 31st March 2027
D. 31st October 2026
Explanation: Under Section 135(6), unspent CSR amount for an ongoing project must be transferred to the 'Unspent CSR Account' within 30 days from the end of the financial year (i.e. within 30 days from 31st March 2026 = 30th April 2026).
Medium SCENARIO · CSR | Section 135 | Ongoing Project Timeframe
Within what maximum timeframe must the amount transferred to the 'Unspent CSR Account' for an ongoing project be actually spent by the company on that project?
A. 1 Financial Year from the transfer
B. 3 Financial Years from the date of transfer ✔
C. 5 Financial Years from the date of transfer
D. Indefinitely without limit
Explanation: Section 135(6) mandates that the unspent CSR amount transferred to the special account must be spent by the company in pursuance of its obligation towards the ongoing project within a period of 3 financial years from the date of such transfer.
Hard SCENARIO · CSR | Section 135 | Schedule VII Fund
If Global Infra Tech Ltd. fails to spend the ₹8 Lakhs within the 3 financial years, what must it do with the remaining unspent amount?
A. Transfer it to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 30 days from the end of the third financial year. ✔
B. Forfeit the amount to the Income Tax Department.
C. Distribute it as dividend to shareholders.
D. Transfer it back to General Reserve.
Explanation: Section 135(6) specifies that failing to spend the amount within 3 financial years requires the company to transfer the unspent amount to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within 30 days from the date of completion of the third financial year.
CASE SCENARIO: Nova Engineering Ltd. suffered a fire accident resulting in a net loss during FY 2025-26. The Board proposes to pay managerial remuneration to its Managing Director, Mr. Vivek. Extract of capital structure as on 31st March 2026: - Paid-up Equity Share Capital: ₹200 Lakhs - Paid-up Preference Share Capital: ₹50 Lakhs - Securities Premium: ₹30 Lakhs - General Reserve: ₹70 Lakhs - Long-Term Bank Loans: ₹150 Lakhs - Cash Credit / Bank Overdraft (repayable on demand): ₹40 Lakhs - Investments in shares of other companies: ₹80 Lakhs - Accumulated Losses (Debit balance of P&L): ₹40 Lakhs - Preliminary Expenses not written off: ₹10 Lakhs
Hard SCENARIO · Schedule V | Effective Capital | Calculation
What is the 'Effective Capital' of Nova Engineering Ltd. for FY 2025-26 under Schedule V Part II?
A. ₹370 Lakhs ✔
B. ₹410 Lakhs
C. ₹320 Lakhs
D. ₹500 Lakhs
Explanation: Effective Capital Computation: + Paid up Equity Share Capital (200) + Paid up Preference Share Capital (50) + Securities Premium (30) + General Reserve (70) + Long-Term Loans (150) [Bank Overdraft is short-term, so excluded] Subtotal = ₹500 Lakhs MINUS: - Investments (80) - Accumulated Losses (40) - Preliminary Expenses (10) Total Deductions = ₹130 Lakhs Effective Capital = 500 - 130 = ₹370 Lakhs (₹3.70 Crores).
Medium SCENARIO · Schedule V | Managerial Remuneration | Limits
Based on the Effective Capital calculated, what is the maximum annual remuneration payable to Mr. Vivek under Schedule V if approved by an ORDINARY RESOLUTION?
A. ₹60 Lakhs
B. ₹84 Lakhs ✔
C. ₹120 Lakhs
D. ₹168 Lakhs
Explanation: Effective Capital = ₹370 Lakhs (₹3.7 Crores), which falls in the slab '₹60 Lakhs and above but less than ₹5 Crores'. For this slab, maximum annual remuneration by Ordinary Resolution is ₹84 Lakhs.
Medium SCENARIO · Schedule V | Special Resolution | Doubled Limit
What is the maximum annual remuneration payable to Mr. Vivek if the shareholders pass a SPECIAL RESOLUTION?
A. ₹84 Lakhs
B. ₹120 Lakhs
C. ₹168 Lakhs ✔
D. ₹200 Lakhs
Explanation: Under Schedule V Part II Section II, the limits specified can be doubled if the company passes a Special Resolution in general meeting. Double of ₹84 Lakhs = ₹168 Lakhs.
Hard SCENARIO · Schedule V | Excess Remuneration | Approval Requirements
If Nova Engineering Ltd. wants to pay Mr. Vivek ₹200 Lakhs per annum (which exceeds the doubled Schedule V limit of ₹168 Lakhs), what approval is required?
A. No further approval needed, Board resolution is final.
B. Central Government approval is not required, but approval of shareholders by Special Resolution along with NOC from creditors/banks (if default exists) is required. ✔
C. Compulsory prior approval from the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
D. Approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
Explanation: Under the amended Companies Act provisions (Schedule V), Central Government approval for excess managerial remuneration has been eliminated. Excess payment requires Special Resolution of shareholders and prior NOC from banks/financial institutions/secured creditors if the company has defaulted in payment of dues.

Paper 1: Advanced Accounting · Module 3 · Chapter 12:

Accounts — 55 rows
Easy NORMAL · Section 68 | Board Resolution Limit | Buyback Thresholds
Under Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the maximum limit up to which a company's Board of Directors can authorize a buy-back of equity shares via a Board Resolution without requiring a Special Resolution in a general meeting?
A. 10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company ✔
B. 10% of the total paid-up equity share capital only
C. 25% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company
D. 25% of the total paid-up equity share capital only
Explanation: Section 68(2) specifies that a special resolution is not required if the buy-back is ten per cent or less of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company, and such buy-back has been authorized by the Board by means of a resolution passed at its meeting.
Easy NORMAL · Section 68 | Equity Capital Limit | Statutory Caps
What is the maximum limit on the buy-back of equity shares in any financial year as per Section 68(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, in respect of paid-up equity capital?
A. 10% of total paid-up equity share capital in that financial year
B. 20% of total paid-up equity share capital in that financial year
C. 25% of total paid-up equity share capital in that financial year ✔
D. 25% of total paid-up equity capital and free reserves combined
Explanation: In respect of the buy-back of equity shares in any financial year, the buy-back cannot exceed 25% of its total paid-up equity capital in that financial year as per the proviso to Section 68(2).
Easy NORMAL · Debt-Equity Ratio | Section 68 | Post-Buyback Ratios
As per Section 68(2)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, what must be the maximum ratio of the aggregate of secured and unsecured debts owed by the company after the buy-back to the paid-up capital and its free reserves?
A. 1:1
B. 1.5:1
C. 2:1 ✔
D. 3:1
Explanation: Section 68(2)(c) mandates that the ratio of the aggregate of secured and unsecured debts owed by the company after buy-back is not more than twice the paid-up capital and its free reserves (i.e., Debt-Equity ratio not exceeding 2:1).
Easy NORMAL · Time Limit | Section 68 | Completion Period
Within what period from the date of passing the Special Resolution (or Board Resolution, as the case may be) must every buy-back of shares be completed?
A. 6 months
B. 12 months ✔
C. 18 months
D. 24 months
Explanation: Section 68(4) provides that every buy-back shall be completed within a period of twelve months from the date of passing the special resolution or the resolution passed by the Board.
Easy NORMAL · Extinction of Shares | Section 68 | Statutory Timelines
According to Section 68(7) of the Companies Act, 2013, within how many days of the completion of the buy-back process must a company extinguish and physically destroy the shares so bought back?
A. 7 days ✔
B. 15 days
C. 21 days
D. 30 days
Explanation: Section 68(7) mandates that where a company buys back its own shares or other specified securities, it shall extinguish and physically destroy the shares or securities so bought back within seven days of the last date of completion of buy-back.
Easy NORMAL · Cooling-off Period | Section 68 | Further Issue Prohibition
Under Section 68(8) of the Companies Act, 2013, after completing a buy-back of shares, a company cannot make a further issue of the same kind of shares within a cooling-off period of:
A. 3 months
B. 6 months ✔
C. 12 months
D. 24 months
Explanation: Section 68(8) prohibits a company from making a further issue of the same kind of shares or other securities including allotment of new shares under Section 62(1)(a) or other specified securities within a period of six months except by way of a bonus issue or discharge of subsisting obligations.
Easy NORMAL · Free Reserves | Capital Redemption Reserve | Revaluation Reserve
Which of the following reserve balances CANNOT be utilized for the creation of Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) upon buy-back of equity shares?
A. General Reserve
B. Profit and Loss Account (Credit balance)
C. Securities Premium Account
D. Revaluation Reserve ✔
Explanation: Revaluation Reserve represents unrealized capital gains and is not a free reserve. Under Section 69, CRR is created out of free reserves or securities premium account.
Easy NORMAL · Capital Redemption Reserve | Bonus Shares | Utilization of CRR
According to Section 69(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) account created on buy-back of shares may be applied by the company in paying up unissued shares to be issued to members as:
A. Sweat equity shares
B. Fully paid bonus shares ✔
C. Rights shares
D. Employee stock options
Explanation: Section 69(2) provides that the Capital Redemption Reserve account may be applied by the company in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares.
Medium NORMAL · CRR Calculation | Fresh Issue | Accounting Treatment
A company proposes to buy back 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹25 per share. It issues 5,000, 10% Preference Shares of ₹10 each at par for the purpose of buy-back. How much amount must be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) account?
A. ₹50,000 ✔
B. ₹1,000,000
C. ₹150,000
D. ₹250,000
Explanation: Nominal value of shares bought back = 10,000 × ₹10 = ₹100,000. Nominal value of fresh issue of preference shares = 5,000 × ₹10 = ₹50,000. Transfer to CRR = Nominal Value of Buyback - Nominal Value of Fresh Issue = ₹100,000 - ₹50,000 = ₹50,000.
Medium NORMAL · Section 68(1) | Sources of Buyback | Prohibition of Same Class
Can a company buy back its equity shares out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of equity shares of the same class?
A. Yes, without any statutory restrictions
B. Yes, provided approval is obtained from SEBI
C. No, Section 68(1) explicitly prohibits buy-back out of proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares ✔
D. Yes, provided a period of 12 months has elapsed since the earlier issue
Explanation: The proviso to Section 68(1) explicitly states that no buy-back of any kind of shares or other specified securities shall be made out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or same kind of other specified securities.
Easy NORMAL · Section 70 | Prohibition of Buyback | Statutory Restrictions
Under Section 70(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company is prohibited from directly or indirectly purchasing its own shares through which of the following?
A. Any subsidiary company including its own subsidiary company
B. Any investment company or group of investment companies
C. If a default is subsisting in repayment of deposits or interest payable thereon
D. All of the above ✔
Explanation: Section 70 prohibits buy-back through any subsidiary company (including its own subsidiary), through any investment company/group of investment companies, or if default is subsisting in repayment of deposits, debentures, preference shares, term loans, or interest thereon.
Medium NORMAL · Section 70 | Curing Defaults | Three-Year Cooling Period
If a company has defaulted in the repayment of a term loan from a financial institution, but subsequently remedies the default and pays off all dues, after what period from the date the default ceased to exist can the company make a buy-back of its shares under Section 70?
A. Immediately upon full repayment
B. 1 year
C. 3 years ✔
D. 5 years
Explanation: The proviso to Section 70(1) states that the prohibition shall not apply if the default is remedied and a period of three years has lapsed after such default ceased to exist.
Medium NORMAL · Free Reserves Definition | Securities Premium | Section 68 Explanation
For the purpose of calculating 'Free Reserves' under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following is specifically included by definition for buy-back calculations?
A. Revaluation Reserve
B. Securities Premium Account ✔
C. Capital Redemption Reserve
D. Debenture Redemption Reserve
Explanation: Explanation to Section 68 explicitly defines 'free reserves' for the purpose of buy-back as including the securities premium account (whereas Sec 2(43) general definition excludes it, Sec 68 explicitly includes securities premium as a source/free reserve component).
Easy NORMAL · Fully Paid Shares | Section 68(2) | Pre-conditions for Buyback
Alpha Ltd. has 100,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 paid up. The company passes a special resolution to buy back 20% of its equity shares at ₹20 per share. Can Alpha Ltd. proceed with this buy-back directly?
A. Yes, provided it creates adequate CRR
B. Yes, as 20% is within the statutory limit of 25%
C. No, because shares must be fully paid up prior to buy-back ✔
D. No, because buy-back cannot exceed 10% without NCLT approval
Explanation: Under Section 68(2)(f), no buy-back of shares shall be made unless all the shares or other specified securities for buy-back are fully paid-up. The company must first make the shares fully paid up.
Medium NORMAL · Premium on Buyback | Accounting Entries | Adjustment of Premium
Beta Ltd. buys back 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹15 per share. Premium on buy-back is ₹5 per share. The company has a Securities Premium balance of ₹80,000 and General Reserve of ₹200,000. What is the correct accounting treatment for the premium paid on buy-back?
A. Debited to Capital Redemption Reserve Account
B. Debited to Profit and Loss Account as an exceptional item
C. Debited to Securities Premium / General Reserve Account ✔
D. Capitalized by issuing bonus shares
Explanation: Premium payable on buy-back is a loss/capital outflow that is provided for out of free reserves or securities premium account before the shares are bought back.
Medium NORMAL · Section 68(8) | Prohibition Exceptions | Bonus Issue
Which of the following is an EXCEPTION to the 6-month prohibition on making further issue of the same kind of shares post buy-back under Section 68(8)?
A. Issue of shares under Rights Issue to existing shareholders
B. Issue of shares under Private Placement
C. Issue of fully paid bonus shares ✔
D. Issue of shares to public via IPO
Explanation: Section 68(8) states that the 6-month restriction does not apply to a bonus issue or discharge of subsisting obligations such as conversion of warrants, stock option schemes, sweat equity, or conversion of preference shares/debentures into equity.
Hard NORMAL · CRR Calculation | Fresh Issue Premium | Section 69
Gama Ltd. decides to buy back 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per share. It issues 30,000 12% Preference shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹5 per share to finance the buy-back. What amount must Gama Ltd. transfer to the Capital Redemption Reserve?
A. ₹200,000 ✔
B. ₹350,000
C. ₹500,000
D. ₹150,000
Explanation: Nominal value of equity shares bought back = 50,000 × ₹10 = ₹500,000. Nominal value of fresh issue = 30,000 × ₹10 = ₹300,000 (premium on fresh issue is ignored for CRR calculation). Transfer to CRR = ₹500,000 - ₹300,000 = ₹200,000.
Medium NORMAL · Section 70(2) | Disqualifications | Statutory Defaults
Which of the following non-compliance scenarios disables a company from making a buy-back of its securities under Section 70(2) of the Companies Act, 2013?
A. Default in filing Annual Return under Section 92
B. Default in distribution of declared dividend under Section 127
C. Default in filing Financial Statements under Section 137
D. All of the above ✔
Explanation: Under Section 70(2), no company shall buy back its shares if it has defaulted in complying with Section 92 (Annual Return), Section 123 (Declaration of Dividend), Section 127 (Punishment for failure to distribute dividend), or Section 137 (Filing of financial statements).
Hard NORMAL · Debt-Equity Test | Maximum Buyback Limit | Financial Testing
Omega Ltd. has Paid-up Share Capital of ₹50 lakhs (Equity share capital of ₹10 each), Free Reserves of ₹30 lakhs, Securities Premium of ₹20 lakhs, and Total Debt of ₹140 lakhs. What is the maximum permitted Debt under the Debt-Equity Test for post-buyback eligibility?
A. Total Debt cannot exceed ₹200 lakhs post buyback
B. Post-buyback aggregate Paid-up Capital and Free Reserves must be at least ₹70 lakhs (half of Total Debt) ✔
C. Post-buyback aggregate Paid-up Capital and Free Reserves must be at least ₹140 lakhs
D. Total Debt must be fully repaid before buyback
Explanation: Under Section 68(2)(c), post buyback Debt-Equity ratio must not exceed 2:1. Aggregate Debt = ₹140 lakhs. Minimum post-buyback Equity (Capital + Free Reserves + Securities Premium) required = ₹140 lakhs / 2 = ₹70 lakhs.
Easy NORMAL · Accounting Entries | Capital Redemption Reserve | Journal Entries
When shares are bought back out of free reserves or securities premium account, which account is credited for the nominal value of the shares bought back?
A. Equity Share Capital Account
B. Capital Redemption Reserve Account ✔
C. General Reserve Account
D. Buy-back Payable Account
Explanation: As per Section 69, when shares are bought back out of free reserves or securities premium account, a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares so purchased shall be transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve Account.
Medium NORMAL · Capital Maintenance Principle | Rationale of CRR | Creditor Protection
What is the primary objective of transferring an amount equal to the face value of shares bought back (out of free reserves) to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR)?
A. To reduce income tax liability of the company
B. To safeguard creditors' interest by maintaining capital intact ✔
C. To enable distribution of cash dividends in future
D. To create a reserve for writing off capital losses
Explanation: The creation of CRR ensures capital maintenance. Since buy-back reduces paid-up share capital, replacing capital with a non-distributable reserve (CRR) protects creditors from capital erosion.
Medium NORMAL · Journal Entries | Payment Entry | Buyback Accounting
Zenith Ltd. buys back its shares at a premium. The accounting entry to record the payment to shareholders is:
A. Debit Equity Shares Buy-back Account; Credit Bank Account
B. Debit Equity Share Capital Account; Credit Bank Account
C. Debit Equity Share Buy-back Holder Account; Credit Bank Account ✔
D. Debit Capital Redemption Reserve; Credit Bank Account
Explanation: The payment entry is: Equity Share Buy-back Holders Account Dr. to Bank Account. (After transferring the buyback liability from Equity Share Capital and Premium on Buyback to Equity Share Buy-back Holders Account).
Easy NORMAL · Section 68(5) | Modes of Buyback | Eligible Sellers
Under Section 68(5), buy-back of securities can be made from which of the following modes?
A. From existing shareholders or security holders on a proportionate basis
B. From the open market
C. By purchasing the securities issued to employees of the company pursuant to a scheme of stock option or sweat equity
D. All of the above ✔
Explanation: Section 68(5) explicitly allows buy-back from existing shareholders on proportionate basis, from open market, or by purchasing securities issued to employees under ESOP or sweat equity.
Hard NORMAL · Net Worth Effect | Balance Sheet Impact | Bonus Issue
If a company buys back shares out of free reserves and subsequently utilizes the whole Capital Redemption Reserve so created to issue fully paid bonus shares, what is the net effect on the total Shareholders' Funds (Net Worth)?
A. Increases by the amount of bonus shares issued
B. Decreases by the total cash outflow spent on buy-back ✔
C. Remains unchanged post buy-back
D. Decreases by double the nominal value of shares bought back
Explanation: The cash payout on buy-back reduces Shareholders' Funds by the total payout amount. The subsequent transfer from CRR to Share Capital for bonus shares is merely an internal reclassification within Shareholders' Funds, having zero net impact on total Shareholders' Funds.
Hard NORMAL · Debenture Redemption Reserve | Free Reserves | Reserve Reclassification
A company has a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) of ₹50,000 created out of profits. The debentures have been fully redeemed. Can this DRR balance be treated as a 'Free Reserve' for the purpose of buy-back under Section 68?
A. No, DRR can never be used for buy-back
B. Yes, once debentures are fully redeemed, DRR can be transferred to General Reserve and used as a free reserve ✔
C. Yes, but only with prior NCLT approval
D. No, DRR must be transferred to Capital Reserve which is not a free reserve
Explanation: Once debentures are redeemed, DRR is no longer restricted and is transferred to General Reserve. General Reserve is a free reserve and hence available for buy-back under Section 68.
Medium NORMAL · Declaration of Solvency | Form SH-9 | Procedural Compliance
Which document is required to be filed with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) and SEBI (in case of listed companies) declaring solvency before undertaking a buy-back?
A. Declaration of Solvency (Form SH-9) ✔
B. Return of Buy-back (Form SH-11)
C. Certificate of Extinction (Form SH-10)
D. Prospectus
Explanation: Under Section 68(6), before making a buy-back, the company must file a Declaration of Solvency in Form SH-9 signed by at least two directors (one of whom shall be the Managing Director, if any) with the ROC and SEBI.
Medium NORMAL · General Reserve Utilization | Accounting Impact | CRR Creation
A company buys back 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹12 per share. Total cash payout = ₹120,000. It funds the buyback using available General Reserve. What is the net reduction in General Reserve as a result of this transaction (including CRR creation and premium write-off)?
A. ₹100,000
B. ₹120,000 ✔
C. ₹20,000
D. ₹140,000
Explanation: Reduction in General Reserve = Transfer to CRR for nominal value (₹100,000) + Premium on buyback written off (10,000 × ₹2 = ₹20,000). Total reduction = ₹100,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹120,000.
Easy NORMAL · Free Reserves Exclusion | Revaluation Reserve | Definitions
Under Section 68, which of the following items is EXCLUDED from 'Free Reserves' when calculating the capacity for buy-back?
A. Securities Premium Account
B. General Reserve
C. Unrealized gains / Capital Reserve arising from revaluation of assets ✔
D. Profit and Loss Account Credit Balance
Explanation: Free reserves as defined in Section 2(43) and Section 68 exclude any amount representing unrealized gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets.
Medium NORMAL · Form SH-11 | Return of Buyback | Procedural Compliance
If a company completes a buy-back on 15th March 2026, what is the mandatory timeline by which Form SH-11 (Return of Buy-back) must be filed with the ROC?
A. Within 7 days (i.e., by 22nd March 2026)
B. Within 30 days (i.e., by 14th April 2026) ✔
C. Within 60 days
D. At the time of filing Annual Return
Explanation: As per Rule 17(10) of Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, the company shall file a return of buy-back in Form SH-11 within 30 days of completion of buy-back with the ROC.
Medium NORMAL · Section 68(8) | Sweat Equity | Exceptions to Cooling-off
Can a company issue Sweat Equity Shares during the 6-month cooling-off period following a buy-back under Section 68(8)?
A. No, all fresh share issuances are strictly prohibited
B. Yes, sweat equity shares are explicitly exempted from the 6-month cooling-off restriction ✔
C. Yes, but only with prior approval of NCLT
D. No, unless authorized by a unanimous resolution of shareholders
Explanation: Section 68(8) proviso explicitly exempts discharge of subsisting obligations such as conversion of warrants, stock option schemes, sweat equity, or conversion of preference shares/debentures from the 6-month restriction.
CASE SCENARIO: PQR Limited (a non-listed public company) presents the following balance sheet summary as on 31st March 2026: - Authorized Share Capital: 2,000,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each = ₹200 lakhs. - Issued and Paid-up Share Capital: 1,000,000 Equity Shares of ₹10 each fully paid = ₹100 lakhs. - Securities Premium Account: ₹40 lakhs. - General Reserve: ₹60 lakhs. - Profit and Loss Account (Cr.): ₹20 lakhs. - Revaluation Reserve: ₹30 lakhs. - 12% Secured Debentures: ₹150 lakhs. - Unsecured Loans: ₹50 lakhs. The company desires to buy back maximum possible equity shares at a offer price of ₹25 per share on 1st April 2026.
Medium SCENARIO · Board Resolution Limit | Section 68 | Buyback Tests
What is the maximum amount of buy-back permitted if authorized solely by a resolution passed at the Board of Directors meeting without shareholder approval?
A. ₹10 lakhs
B. ₹22 lakhs ✔
C. ₹25 lakhs
D. ₹12 lakhs
Explanation: Board limit = 10% of (Paid-up equity capital + Free Reserves including Securities Premium). Paid-up equity capital = ₹100 lakhs. Free Reserves = Securities Premium (₹40 lakhs) + General Reserve (₹60 lakhs) + P&L Cr. (₹20 lakhs) = ₹120 lakhs. (Revaluation reserve excluded). Total base = ₹100 + ₹120 = ₹220 lakhs. Board limit = 10% of ₹220 lakhs = ₹22 lakhs.
Medium SCENARIO · 25% Equity Limit | Section 68 | Number of Shares Test
What is the maximum number of equity shares that can be bought back under the 25% Equity Share Capital test (Section 68(2)(c) proviso) for the financial year?
A. 100,000 equity shares
B. 220,000 equity shares
C. 250,000 equity shares ✔
D. 500,000 equity shares
Explanation: 25% of Paid-up Equity Share Capital test = 25% of 1,000,000 shares = 250,000 shares.
Hard SCENARIO · Debt-Equity Test | Section 68(2)(c) | Financial Constraints
Under the Debt-Equity Ratio test, what is the maximum permissible buy-back amount that PQR Limited can spend at ₹25 per share?
A. ₹120 lakhs
B. ₹100 lakhs
C. ₹120 lakhs maximum limit but restricted by equity maintenance of ₹100 lakhs ✔
D. ₹120 lakhs total equity minus minimum equity required (₹100 lakhs) = ₹120 lakhs capacity
Explanation: Total Debt = 12% Secured Debentures (₹150 lakhs) + Unsecured Loans (₹50 lakhs) = ₹200 lakhs. Minimum post-buyback Equity (Capital + Free Reserves) required = Total Debt / 2 = ₹200 lakhs / 2 = ₹100 lakhs. Present Equity (Capital + Free Reserves) = ₹100 + ₹120 = ₹220 lakhs. Maximum allowable reduction in Equity under Debt-Equity test = Present Equity - Minimum Equity required = ₹220 lakhs - ₹100 lakhs = ₹120 lakhs.
Hard SCENARIO · Comprehensive Buyback Test | Maximum Buyback Shares | Section 68
Considering the Shareholder Approval overall 25% limit on Paid-up Capital + Free Reserves (25% of ₹220 lakhs = ₹55 lakhs) and the Debt-Equity test (₹120 lakhs) and 25% Equity shares limit (250,000 shares @ ₹25 = ₹62.5 lakhs), what is the MAXIMUM number of equity shares PQR Ltd. can buy back at ₹25 per share after passing a Special Resolution?
A. 220,000 shares ✔
B. 250,000 shares
C. 200,000 shares
D. 240,000 shares
Explanation: Test 1: Shareholder Approval limit (25% of Capital + Free Reserves) = 25% of ₹220 lakhs = ₹55 lakhs. At ₹25 per share, Number of shares = ₹55,000,000 / ₹25 = 220,000 shares. Test 2: 25% Equity share limit = 250,000 shares. Test 3: Debt-Equity Test = ₹120 lakhs / ₹25 = 480,000 shares. The maximum allowed is the lowest of all three tests, which is 220,000 shares.
CASE SCENARIO: Vanguard Limited decides to buy back 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price of ₹30 per share on 15th May 2026. The balances in its accounts prior to buy-back are: - Securities Premium Account: ₹500,000 - General Reserve: ₹800,000 - Profit and Loss Account (Cr.): ₹300,000 To finance part of the buy-back, Vanguard Ltd. makes a fresh issue of 20,000, 10% Preference Shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 20% ( issue price ₹12 per share) on 10th May 2026, which is fully subscribed and paid.
Medium SCENARIO · Nominal Value | Premium on Buyback | Buyback Calculations
What is the total nominal value of equity shares bought back and the total premium paid on buy-back by Vanguard Ltd.?
A. Nominal Value = ₹400,000; Premium on Buy-back = ₹800,000 ✔
B. Nominal Value = ₹400,000; Premium on Buy-back = ₹1,200,000
C. Nominal Value = ₹200,000; Premium on Buy-back = ₹600,000
D. Nominal Value = ₹800,000; Premium on Buy-back = ₹400,000
Explanation: Nominal value = 40,000 shares × ₹10 = ₹400,000. Buyback price = ₹30 per share. Premium on buyback = 40,000 shares × (₹30 - ₹10) = ₹800,000.
Hard SCENARIO · CRR Calculation | Fresh Issue of Shares | Section 69
How much amount must Vanguard Ltd. transfer to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) Account upon buy-back?
A. ₹400,000
B. ₹200,000 ✔
C. ₹160,000
D. ₹240,000
Explanation: Nominal value of equity shares bought back = ₹400,000. Nominal value of fresh issue of preference shares = 20,000 × ₹10 = ₹200,000. (Premium on fresh issue ₹40,000 is ignored for CRR computation). Transfer to CRR = Nominal Value of Buyback - Nominal Value of Fresh Issue = ₹400,000 - ₹200,000 = ₹200,000.
Hard SCENARIO · Securities Premium Adjustment | Premium Write-off | Accounting Entries
What is the balance remaining in the Securities Premium Account after providing for premium on buy-back and receiving premium on fresh issue?
A. ₹0 ✔
B. ₹260,000
C. ₹540,000
D. ₹100,000
Explanation: Initial Securities Premium = ₹500,000. Add: Premium on fresh issue (20,000 × ₹2) = ₹40,000. Total Securities Premium available = ₹540,000. Total premium on buy-back required = ₹800,000. Entire ₹540,000 of Securities Premium is utilized towards writing off buy-back premium, leaving a balance of ₹0. (The remaining ₹260,000 buyback premium will be written off against General Reserve).
Hard SCENARIO · General Reserve Balance | Post-Buyback Reserves | Comprehensive Accounting
What is the balance remaining in the General Reserve Account after making all required adjustments for buy-back and CRR creation?
A. ₹340,000 ✔
B. ₹540,000
C. ₹600,000
D. ₹800,000
Explanation: Initial General Reserve = ₹800,000. Amount used for remaining premium on buy-back = ₹260,000 (since total premium was ₹800,000 and Securities Premium covered ₹540,000). Amount used for CRR transfer = ₹200,000. Balance remaining in General Reserve = ₹800,000 - ₹260,000 - ₹200,000 = ₹340,000.
CASE SCENARIO: Kriti Ltd. is contemplating a buy-back of equity shares in June 2026. On reviewing its corporate records, the statutory auditor highlights the following issues: 1. Kriti Ltd. holds 100% equity in S1 Ltd. It is proposed that S1 Ltd. will purchase 5% of Kriti Ltd.'s equity shares from the stock market on behalf of Kriti Ltd. 2. Kriti Ltd. defaulted in repayment of interest on a bank term loan in 2022. The default was fully cleared with all penalties on 31st March 2023. 3. Kriti Ltd. has failed to file its Financial Statements under Section 137 for the financial year ended 31st March 2025.
Easy SCENARIO · Section 70 | Subsidiary Buyback Prohibition | Statutory Restrictions
Regarding Point 1 (purchase of shares through subsidiary S1 Ltd.), is this mode of buy-back permissible under the Companies Act, 2013?
A. Yes, provided S1 Ltd. passes a special resolution
B. Yes, because S1 Ltd. is a wholly owned subsidiary
C. No, Section 70(1)(a) strictly prohibits buy-back through any subsidiary company including its own subsidiary ✔
D. Yes, provided approval is taken from SEBI
Explanation: Section 70(1)(a) explicitly states that no company shall directly or indirectly purchase its own shares through any subsidiary company including its own subsidiary company.
Medium SCENARIO · Section 70 Proviso | Default Remedy Period | Three-Year Rule
Regarding Point 2 (default in bank loan interest cleared on 31st March 2023), is Kriti Ltd. eligible to proceed with a buy-back in June 2026 under Section 70?
A. No, because default once committed permanently debars the company from buy-back
B. Yes, because a period of 3 years has lapsed since the default ceased to exist on 31st March 2023 ✔
C. No, because 5 years must elapse from the date of default remedy
D. Yes, because interest defaults are exempted under Section 70
Explanation: Under the proviso to Section 70(1), the prohibition on buy-back does not apply if the default is remedied and a period of 3 years has lapsed after such default ceased to exist. From 31st March 2023 to June 2026, 3 years have completed.
Medium SCENARIO · Section 70(2) | Non-compliance Disqualification | Section 137 Default
Regarding Point 3 (failure to file Financial Statements under Section 137 for FY 2024-25), how does this affect Kriti Ltd.'s buy-back proposal in June 2026?
A. It has no impact as long as tax returns are filed
B. Section 70(2) prohibits buy-back if default in Section 137 exists; Kriti Ltd. cannot buy back shares until rectified ✔
C. Kriti Ltd. can buy back up to 10% under Board resolution despite default
D. Kriti Ltd. can proceed if it pays a penalty of ₹10,000 to ROC
Explanation: Section 70(2) specifies that no company shall buy back its shares if default is made in complying with Section 92, 123, 127, or 137. Thus, default under Section 137 debars the company.
Hard SCENARIO · Comprehensive Disqualification | Section 70 Compliance | Legal Conclusion
What is the ultimate legal position regarding Kriti Ltd.'s proposal to buy back its equity shares in June 2026 in its present condition?
A. Kriti Ltd. can proceed immediately as 3 years have passed since term loan default
B. Kriti Ltd. cannot proceed because of non-compliance with Section 137 and prohibition of buyback through subsidiary ✔
C. Kriti Ltd. can proceed if it buys back directly and not through S1 Ltd.
D. Kriti Ltd. requires prior approval from NCLT to proceed
Explanation: Even though the term loan default 3-year cooling period has passed, Kriti Ltd. cannot proceed because (i) buyback through subsidiary S1 Ltd. is prohibited under Sec 70(1)(a), and (ii) default under Sec 137 is subsisting under Sec 70(2). Both must be rectified (buyback directly + file financial statements) before executing buyback.
CASE SCENARIO: Apex Ltd. wants to buy back 100,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at par on 1st April 2025 out of its General Reserve ( balance ₹500,000). The buy-back is completed and shares extinguished on 5th April 2025. On 1st October 2025 (6 months after buy-back), Apex Ltd. wants to execute two capital actions: 1. Issue fully paid bonus shares in the ratio of 1 bonus share for every 2 equity shares using the Capital Redemption Reserve created during the buy-back. 2. Make a fresh rights issue of equity shares of the same class to existing shareholders.
Easy SCENARIO · Section 68(7) | Extinction Timeline | 7-Day Rule
By which date must Apex Ltd. complete the physical destruction/extinction of the 100,000 shares bought back on 1st April 2025?
A. 8th April 2025 ✔
B. 12th April 2025
C. 15th April 2025
D. 30th April 2025
Explanation: Section 68(7) requires extinction and physical destruction of shares bought back within 7 days of the last date of completion of buy-back. If buy-back completed on 1st April, deadline is 8th April 2025.
Medium SCENARIO · CRR Creation | Section 69(2) | Bonus Share Issuance
How much amount was transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) on 1st April 2025, and can CRR be utilized on 1st October 2025 for issuing fully paid bonus shares?
A. CRR = ₹1,000,000; Yes, Section 69(2) explicitly allows CRR to be used for issuing fully paid bonus shares ✔
B. CRR = ₹1,000,000; No, CRR cannot be used within 12 months of buy-back
C. CRR = ₹500,000; Yes, but only up to General Reserve balance
D. CRR = ₹0; Buy-back at par does not require CRR
Explanation: Nominal value of buy-back = 100,000 × ₹10 = ₹1,000,000. Transfer to CRR = ₹1,000,000. Under Section 69(2), CRR can be utilized for issuing fully paid bonus shares without any time barrier.
Hard SCENARIO · Section 68(8) | Cooling-off Expiry | Rights Issue
Is the proposed fresh Rights Issue of equity shares on 1st October 2025 legally permissible under Section 68(8)?
A. Yes, because 6 months have passed since 1st April 2025 ✔
B. No, because a 12-month prohibition applies to rights issues
C. Yes, because rights issues are exempt from the 6-month restriction under all circumstances
D. No, because rights issues require NCLT clearance post buyback
Explanation: Section 68(8) prohibits further issue of the same kind of shares within a period of six months. The buyback was on 1st April 2025; 6 months lapse on 1st October 2025. Hence, the rights issue proposed on 1st October 2025 is legally permissible.
Medium SCENARIO · Bonus Share Entries | CRR Utilization | Journal Entries
What is the accounting entry passed when CRR is utilized to issue fully paid bonus shares?
A. Debit Capital Redemption Reserve A/c; Credit Bonus to Shareholders A/c (and subsequently Debit Bonus to Shareholders A/c; Credit Equity Share Capital A/c) ✔
B. Debit Equity Share Capital A/c; Credit Capital Redemption Reserve A/c
C. Debit General Reserve A/c; Credit Capital Redemption Reserve A/c
D. Debit Profit & Loss A/c; Credit Equity Share Capital A/c
Explanation: When bonus shares are issued out of CRR, the entries are: (1) Capital Redemption Reserve A/c Dr. To Bonus to Shareholders A/c; (2) Bonus to Shareholders A/c Dr. To Equity Share Capital A/c.
CASE SCENARIO: Titanium Ltd. presents the following Extract of Balance Sheet as on 31st March 2026: - Equity Share Capital (Shares of ₹10 each fully paid): ₹500,000 - General Reserve: ₹200,000 - Securities Premium: ₹100,000 - Profit & Loss Account (Cr.): ₹100,000 - Capital Reserve (realized in cash): ₹50,000 - Infrastructure Development Reserve (Statutory Reserve): ₹80,000 - Secured Loan (10% Debentures): ₹600,000 - Unsecured Trade Payables & Short-term Loans: ₹200,000 The company plans to buy back 20% of its equity shares at ₹25 per share.
Medium SCENARIO · Free Reserves Computation | Section 68 | Inclusions and Exclusions
What is the total amount of 'Free Reserves' available for Section 68 buy-back capacity calculation (including Securities Premium)?
A. ₹400,000 ✔
B. ₹450,000
C. ₹530,000
D. ₹300,000
Explanation: Free reserves under Section 68 include General Reserve (₹200,000) + P&L Cr. (₹100,000) + Securities Premium (₹100,000) = ₹400,000. Statutory reserve (Infrastructure Development Reserve) is not free. Capital reserve is generally excluded unless specifically allowed, but under standard Sec 68 rules, free reserves + securities premium = ₹400,000.
Medium SCENARIO · 25% Total Limit Test | Section 68 | Maximum Buyback Limit
What is the maximum aggregate buy-back expenditure allowed under the Shareholder Approval 25% Total Limit Test (25% of Paid-up Capital + Free Reserves)?
A. ₹225,000 ✔
B. ₹125,000
C. ₹200,000
D. ₹180,000
Explanation: Paid-up Share Capital = ₹500,000. Free Reserves (including Securities Premium) = ₹400,000. Aggregate = ₹900,000. 25% of ₹900,000 = ₹225,000.
Hard SCENARIO · Debt-Equity Ratio Test | Minimum Post-Buyback Equity | Section 68(2)(c)
What is the minimum post-buyback Equity required to satisfy the 2:1 Debt-Equity ratio test?
A. ₹400,000 ✔
B. ₹300,000
C. ₹800,000
D. ₹500,000
Explanation: Total Debt = Secured Debentures (₹600,000) + Unsecured Payables/Loans (₹200,000) = ₹800,000. Minimum post-buyback Equity required = Total Debt / 2 = ₹800,000 / 2 = ₹400,000.
Hard SCENARIO · Statutory Test Verification | Section 68 Compliance | Buyback Capacity
If Titanium Ltd. buys back 10,000 equity shares (20% of 50,000 shares) at ₹25 per share (Total cost = ₹250,000), does this proposed buy-back pass ALL statutory tests?
A. Yes, it satisfies all tests
B. No, it fails the 25% total limit test because ₹250,000 exceeds maximum allowable ₹225,000 ✔
C. No, it fails the Debt-Equity test
D. No, because 20% buy-back cannot be made in a single year
Explanation: The maximum permitted outflow under 25% of (Capital + Free Reserves) is ₹225,000. Buying back 10,000 shares at ₹25 costs ₹250,000, which exceeds ₹225,000. Thus, it fails the Shareholder Approval 25% overall limit test.

Paper 1: Advanced Accounting · Module 3 · Chapter 13:

Accounts — 55 rows
Easy NORMAL · AS 14 | Purchase Consideration | Scope of Consideration
According to AS 14 'Accounting for Amalgamations', which of the following payments made by the transferee company is included in the computation of 'Consideration'?
A. Payment made directly to the debenture holders of the transferor company
B. Payment made to the liquidation expense creditors of the transferor company
C. Payment made to the preference shareholders of the transferor company ✔
D. Payment made to the trade creditors of the transferor company
Explanation: As per paragraph 3(b) of AS 14, consideration for amalgamation is the aggregate of the shares and other securities issued and the payment made in cash or other assets by the transferee company to the shareholders (equity and preference) of the transferor company. Payments made to third parties like debenture holders or creditors are settlements of liabilities and not part of purchase consideration.
Easy NORMAL · AS 14 | Amalgamation in Nature of Merger | Conditions for Merger
Under AS 14, which condition MUST be satisfied for an amalgamation to be classified as an 'amalgamation in the nature of merger'?
A. All equity shareholders of the transferor company must become shareholders of the transferee company.
B. Shareholders holding not less than 90% of the face value of equity shares of the transferor company (other than held by transferee/subsidiaries) become equity shareholders of the transferee company. ✔
C. Assets and liabilities must be recorded at fair values in the books of the transferee company.
D. Consideration must be paid entirely in cash to all equity shareholders.
Explanation: Under AS 14, one of the five essential conditions for an amalgamation in the nature of merger is that equity shareholders holding not less than 90% of the face value of equity shares of the transferor company (other than those already held by the transferee company or its subsidiaries) become equity shareholders of the transferee company by virtue of amalgamation.
Easy NORMAL · Pooling of Interests Method | Book Values | AS 14
Under the 'Pooling of Interests Method', how are the assets and liabilities of the transferor company recorded in the books of the transferee company?
A. At their fair values as on the date of amalgamation
B. At their liquidation values as determined by independent valuers
C. At their existing book values, except for adjustments to achieve uniform accounting policies ✔
D. At replacement costs as on the date of acquisition
Explanation: Under paragraph 10 of AS 14 (Pooling of Interests Method), assets, liabilities, and reserves of the transferor company are recorded by the transferee company at their existing carrying amounts (book values), subject only to adjustments required to ensure uniformity of accounting policies.
Easy NORMAL · Purchase Method | Goodwill | Capital Reserve
When an amalgamation is accounted for under the 'Purchase Method', any excess of consideration paid over the net aggregate value of identifiable assets taken over over liabilities assumed is credited or debited to which account?
A. Debited to Capital Reserve Account
B. Debited to Goodwill Account ✔
C. Credited to Amalgamation Adjustment Deficit Account
D. Debited to General Reserve Account
Explanation: Under the Purchase Method of AS 14, if the purchase consideration exceeds the net agreed value of assets taken over less liabilities assumed, the difference is debited to Goodwill Account. If the consideration is less than net assets, the difference is credited to Capital Reserve Account.
Medium NORMAL · Statutory Reserve | Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve | Schedule III
How is the 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve' account presented in the balance sheet of the transferee company prepared as per Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013?
A. As a separate line item under 'Other Non-Current Assets'
B. As a negative line item under 'Reserves and Surplus' ✔
C. Under 'Other Current Assets' as a temporary debit balance
D. Deducted directly from Capital Reserve on the face of the Balance Sheet
Explanation: As per ICAI study material and Schedule III guidelines, when a statutory reserve is maintained under the purchase method, the Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve (or Amalgamation Adjustment Deficit) is presented under 'Reserves and Surplus' as a negative balance (deduction), until the statutory reserve itself is maintained.
Medium NORMAL · Purchase Method | Statutory Reserve | Journal Entries
Alpha Ltd acquires Beta Ltd under the purchase method. Beta Ltd has a statutory reserve (Export Profit Reserve) of ₹1,50,000 which needs to be maintained for 3 more years. What entry is passed in the books of Alpha Ltd?
A. General Reserve A/c Dr. ₹1,50,000 To Export Profit Reserve A/c ₹1,50,000
B. Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c Dr. ₹1,50,000 To Export Profit Reserve A/c ₹1,50,000 ✔
C. Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹1,50,000 To Export Profit Reserve A/c ₹1,50,000
D. No entry is required as statutory reserves are not recorded under the purchase method.
Explanation: Under the purchase method, statutory reserves of the transferor company must be retained by debiting 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve Account' and crediting the relevant 'Statutory Reserve Account' (e.g., Export Profit Reserve).
Medium NORMAL · Liquidation Expenses | Purchase Method | Goodwill/Capital Reserve
When liquidation expenses of the transferor company are paid and borne by the transferee company in an 'amalgamation in the nature of purchase', how is this transaction accounted for in the transferee company's books?
A. Debited to Profit and Loss Account
B. Debited to Realisation Account
C. Debited to Goodwill Account or credited/adjusted in Capital Reserve Account ✔
D. Debited to General Reserve Account
Explanation: In an amalgamation in the nature of purchase, liquidation expenses borne by the transferee company form part of the acquisition cost and are debited to Goodwill Account (or credited/deducted from Capital Reserve Account if capital reserve exists).
Medium NORMAL · Liquidation Expenses | Merger Method | Accounting Treatment
If liquidation expenses of the transferor company are borne by the transferee company in an 'amalgamation in the nature of merger', where should the transferee company debit this expenditure?
A. Goodwill Account
B. Profit and Loss Account or General Reserve ✔
C. Realisation Account
D. Preliminary Expenses Account
Explanation: In an amalgamation in the nature of merger (Pooling of Interests Method), any costs directly incurred by the transferee company to effect amalgamation (including liquidation expenses reimbursed) are debited to Profit and Loss Account or Reserves.
Medium NORMAL · Purchase Consideration | Net Payment Method | Valuation
X Ltd agreed to acquire Y Ltd. X Ltd agreed to issue 3 equity shares of ₹10 each (market price ₹15) for every 5 equity shares in Y Ltd. Y Ltd has 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. Calculate the total Purchase Consideration under AS 14 using the Net Payment Method.
A. ₹6,00,000
B. ₹9,00,000 ✔
C. ₹10,00,000
D. ₹15,00,000
Explanation: Number of shares to be issued = (1,00,000 / 5) * 3 = 60,000 equity shares. Value of shares issued for consideration = 60,000 shares * ₹15 (issue price/agreed value) = ₹9,00,000. Purchase consideration is evaluated based on agreed issue price/value of securities offered.
Medium NORMAL · Purchase Consideration | Net Payment Method | Cash and Share Component
P Ltd takes over Q Ltd. P Ltd agrees to issue 2 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹5 per share for every 4 equity shares in Q Ltd, and pay ₹2 cash per equity share held in Q Ltd. Q Ltd has 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each fully paid. Compute the Purchase Consideration.
A. ₹4,75,000 ✔
B. ₹3,75,000
C. ₹2,50,000
D. ₹1,00,000
Explanation: Equity shares issued = (50,000 / 4) * 2 = 25,000 shares. Value of shares issued = 25,000 * ₹15 = ₹3,75,000. Cash paid = 50,000 * ₹2 = ₹1,00,000. Total Purchase Consideration = ₹3,75,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹4,75,000.
Easy NORMAL · Transferor Company Books | Realisation Account | Closure of Books
In the books of the Transferor Company, where is the carrying value of assets transferred to the transferee company transferred upon liquidation?
A. Debit of Transferee Company's Account
B. Debit of Realisation Account ✔
C. Credit of Realisation Account
D. Debit of Equity Shareholders' Account
Explanation: When closing the books of the transferor company, all asset accounts taken over (or to be realised) are closed by transferring their book values to the debit side of the Realisation Account.
Medium NORMAL · Transferor Company Books | Realisation Account | Preference Shareholders
How is preference share capital settled in the books of the Transferor Company if preference shareholders are paid more than their book value?
A. The excess amount is debited to General Reserve Account.
B. The excess amount is debited to Realisation Account. ✔
C. The excess amount is credited to Profit and Loss Account.
D. The excess amount is debited to Goodwill Account.
Explanation: Any excess paid to preference shareholders over their carrying value represents a loss on settlement, which is debited to Realisation Account in the books of the transferor company.
Medium NORMAL · Purchase Method | Goodwill Calculation | Net Agreed Assets
Sun Ltd acquires Moon Ltd under the purchase method. Net Agreed Assets taken over are ₹12,00,000 and total liabilities assumed are ₹3,00,000. Purchase consideration payable is ₹10,00,000. What is the amount of Goodwill or Capital Reserve resulting from this transaction?
A. Goodwill of ₹1,00,000 ✔
B. Capital Reserve of ₹1,00,000
C. Goodwill of ₹2,00,000
D. Capital Reserve of ₹2,00,000
Explanation: Net Assets taken over = Agreed Assets (₹12,00,000) - Liabilities assumed (₹3,00,000) = ₹9,00,000. Purchase Consideration = ₹10,00,000. Since PC (₹10,00,000) > Net Assets (₹9,00,000), Goodwill = ₹10,00,000 - ₹9,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.
Medium NORMAL · Pooling of Interests Method | Reserve Adjustment | AS 14
Under the Pooling of Interests Method, if the Purchase Consideration paid exceeds the paid-up share capital of the Transferor Company, how is the difference adjusted in the transferee company's books?
A. Debited to Goodwill Account
B. Debited to Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve Account
C. Deducted from Reserves (General Reserve/Capital Reserve/P&L) of the Transferee Company ✔
D. Credited to Capital Reserve Account
Explanation: Under the Pooling of Interests Method, any difference between the amount recorded as share capital issued plus any additional consideration in other forms and the amount of share capital of the transferor company should be adjusted in Reserves (General Reserve or other revenue/capital reserves).
Hard NORMAL · Unrealized Profit | Inter-company Inventory | Purchase Method
Prior to amalgamation, Transferee Ltd sold goods costing ₹80,000 to Transferor Ltd for ₹1,00,000. Half of these goods remain unsold in the inventory of Transferor Ltd on the date of amalgamation. If amalgamation is under the purchase method, what adjustment entry is made in Transferee Ltd's books post-amalgamation for unrealized profit?
A. Goodwill / Capital Reserve A/c Dr. ₹10,000 To Inventory A/c ₹10,000 ✔
B. Profit and Loss A/c Dr. ₹20,000 To Inventory A/c ₹20,000
C. Inventory A/c Dr. ₹10,000 To Goodwill A/c ₹10,000
D. Realisation A/c Dr. ₹10,000 To Profit and Loss A/c ₹10,000
Explanation: Unrealized profit in stock = (₹1,00,000 - ₹80,000) * 50% = ₹10,000. Under the purchase method, post-amalgamation adjustment for unrealized profit on stock included in transferee's inventory is debited to Goodwill / Capital Reserve (or Profit & Loss/General Reserve) and credited to Inventory.
Hard NORMAL · Inter-company Holding | Purchase Consideration | Net Payment Method
Company A absorbs Company B. Company A holds 20% equity shares of Company B prior to amalgamation. How is this existing holding treated when calculating Purchase Consideration under Net Payment Method?
A. Consideration is calculated for 100% shares and 20% is paid to Company A itself.
B. Consideration is calculated only for the 80% shares held by outside shareholders. ✔
C. Consideration is calculated for 100% shares and then 20% is credited to Realisation Account.
D. Consideration is ignored and Net Asset method must be mandatorily applied.
Explanation: When the transferee company already holds shares in the transferor company, no payment (shares/cash) is made to itself. Thus, purchase consideration under Net Payment method is computed only for the shares held by outside shareholders (80%).
Easy NORMAL · Pooling of Interests Method | Preservation of Reserves | Merger
In an amalgamation in the nature of merger, Transferor Ltd has General Reserve of ₹2,00,000, Profit & Loss A/c (Cr.) of ₹1,00,000, and Statutory Reserve of ₹50,000. Which of these reserves are incorporated in the transferee company's books?
A. Only Statutory Reserve of ₹50,000
B. Only General Reserve and Profit & Loss A/c totaling ₹3,00,000
C. All reserves (General Reserve, Profit & Loss A/c, and Statutory Reserve) amounting to ₹3,50,000 ✔
D. None of the reserves are incorporated; all are credited to Capital Reserve.
Explanation: Under the Pooling of Interests method (merger), all reserves (whether capital reserves, revenue reserves, or statutory reserves) of the transferor company are preserved and recorded in the books of the transferee company at their book values.
Easy NORMAL · AS 14 | Purchase Consideration | Debentures Settlement
When debentures of the transferor company are taken over and settled by the transferee company by issuing its own 12% Debentures at a 10% premium, how is this handled in computing Purchase Consideration under AS 14?
A. The value of debentures issued is added to Purchase Consideration.
B. The premium on debentures is added to Purchase Consideration.
C. Debentures issued are ignored in Purchase Consideration as it is a settlement of liability. ✔
D. Only the nominal value of debentures is included in Purchase Consideration.
Explanation: Under AS 14, consideration is payment made to SHAREHOLDERS only. Discharge of debenture holders is a settlement of a liability assumed, not part of purchase consideration.
Medium NORMAL · Statutory Reserve | Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve | Reversal Entry
What happens to 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve' when the statutory requirement to maintain the statutory reserve of the transferor company expires?
A. It is transferred to General Reserve.
B. It is transferred to Capital Reserve.
C. It is reversed by crediting Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve and debiting Statutory Reserve. ✔
D. It is written off to Profit and Loss Account as an exceptional item.
Explanation: When the statutory reserve is no longer required to be maintained by law, both the Statutory Reserve Account and the Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve Account are closed by passing a reversal entry: Statutory Reserve A/c Dr. To Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c.
Hard NORMAL · Purchase Consideration | Net Payment Method | Equity and Preference
Star Ltd acquired Moon Ltd. Equity share capital of Moon Ltd consists of 1,00,000 shares of ₹10 each. Star Ltd issues 1 share of ₹10 (market value ₹20) for every 2 shares of Moon Ltd. Equity shareholders of Moon Ltd also receive cash of ₹3 per share. Preference shareholders (10,00,000 10% Preference shares of ₹10 each) receive 11% Preference shares of Star Ltd of equal value. What is the total Purchase Consideration?
A. ₹23,00,000 ✔
B. ₹13,00,000
C. ₹20,00,000
D. ₹18,00,000
Explanation: Equity Shareholders receive: Shares = (1,00,000 / 2) * 1 = 50,000 shares * ₹20 = ₹10,00,000. Cash = 1,00,000 * ₹3 = ₹3,00,000. Preference Shareholders receive: Preference shares = ₹10,00,000. Total PC = ₹10,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 + ₹10,00,000 = ₹23,00,000.
Easy NORMAL · Net Asset Method | Fictitious Assets | Purchase Consideration
Under the Net Asset Method of computing purchase consideration, which of the following assets of the transferor company should NOT be included in total agreed assets taken over?
A. Unrecorded Patent Rights having commercial value
B. Prepaid Expenses
C. Fictitious Assets like preliminary expenses and debit balance of P&L account ✔
D. Trade Receivables at net realisable value
Explanation: Fictitious assets (such as unamortized preliminary expenses, underwriting commission, or debit balance of P&L account) have no realisable value and are not assets taken over by the transferee company. They are transferred to Equity Shareholders' Account in transferor's books.
Easy NORMAL · Transferor Company Books | Realisation Loss | Equity Shareholders
In the books of the Transferor Company, if Realisation Account shows a debit balance (loss on realisation), how is this loss closed?
A. Credited to Realisation A/c and debited to Equity Shareholders' A/c ✔
B. Debited to Realisation A/c and credited to Capital Reserve A/c
C. Debited to Transferee Company A/c and credited to Realisation A/c
D. Debited to Profit and Loss A/c and credited to Realisation A/c
Explanation: Any profit or loss on realisation belongs to the ultimate owners, i.e., equity shareholders. A realisation loss (debit balance) is closed by crediting Realisation Account and debiting Equity Shareholders' Account.
Medium NORMAL · Intrinsic Value Method | Share Exchange Ratio | Purchase Consideration
A Ltd acquired B Ltd. Equity intrinsic value per share of A Ltd is ₹50 and B Ltd is ₹25. B Ltd has 40,000 equity shares. Based on intrinsic values, what is the exchange ratio and total number of A Ltd shares to be issued to B Ltd shareholders?
A. Ratio 2:1; 80,000 shares issued
B. Ratio 1:2; 20,000 shares issued ✔
C. Ratio 1:1; 40,000 shares issued
D. Ratio 1:4; 10,000 shares issued
Explanation: Exchange ratio = Intrinsic value of B Ltd / Intrinsic value of A Ltd = ₹25 / ₹50 = 0.5 (i.e., 1 share of A Ltd for every 2 shares of B Ltd). Number of shares issued = 40,000 * (1/2) = 20,000 shares of A Ltd.
Easy NORMAL · Mutual Owings | Inter-company Balances | Cancellation
If there is a mutual debt (inter-company debtor/creditor balance of ₹50,000) between Transferor Ltd and Transferee Ltd, how is it eliminated in the books of Transferee Ltd after amalgamation?
A. Debtors A/c Dr. ₹50,000 To Creditors A/c ₹50,000
B. Sundry Creditors A/c Dr. ₹50,000 To Sundry Debtors A/c ₹50,000 ✔
C. Realisation A/c Dr. ₹50,000 To Sundry Debtors A/c ₹50,000
D. General Reserve A/c Dr. ₹50,000 To Sundry Debtors A/c ₹50,000
Explanation: Mutual debts are eliminated in the transferee company's books after recording assets and liabilities by debiting Sundry Creditors and crediting Sundry Debtors with the common/mutual amount.
Medium NORMAL · Net Asset Method | Existing Goodwill | Agreed Value
In an amalgamation in the nature of purchase, existing Goodwill standing in the balance sheet of the Transferor Company is ₹1,00,000. It is taken over at agreed value of ₹80,000. How is this ₹80,000 treated while computing Net Assets taken over by the transferee?
A. Included as an asset at ₹80,000 in computing Net Agreed Assets ✔
B. Ignored completely while calculating Net Agreed Assets
C. Deducted from Capital Reserve
D. Transferred directly to Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve
Explanation: If existing goodwill is taken over at an agreed valuation (₹80,000), it is treated as an identifiable asset taken over at that agreed value while calculating Net Agreed Assets for goodwill/capital reserve determination.
Easy NORMAL · Fractional Shares | Cash Settlement | AS 14
When fractional shares arise in calculating share entitlement on amalgamation, how are they typically settled by the transferee company?
A. By issuing bonus equity shares
B. In cash based on the market/agreed value of shares ✔
C. By ignoring the fractional entitlement completely
D. By issuing preference shares of equal nominal value
Explanation: As per AS 14, consideration includes cash paid for fractional shares. Fractional entitlements are settled in cash based on the issue/market price of the transferee company's shares.
Hard NORMAL · Mutual Owings | Discounted Bills | Inter-company Cancellation
X Ltd acquires Y Ltd. The trade bills accepted by Y Ltd include ₹30,000 drawn by X Ltd. Prior to amalgamation, X Ltd had discounted ₹10,000 of these bills with its bank. What amount of Bills Payable and Bills Receivable should be cancelled upon amalgamation in X Ltd's books?
A. ₹30,000
B. ₹20,000 ✔
C. ₹10,000
D. Nil
Explanation: Out of ₹30,000 bills, ₹10,000 was discounted with the bank (so X Ltd no longer holds the Bills Receivable for that ₹10,000). The mutual B/R and B/P held internally between X Ltd and Y Ltd is only ₹20,000. Therefore, only ₹20,000 is cancelled.
Easy NORMAL · AS 14 | Conditions for Merger | Purchase Method Classification
If the business of the transferor company is NOT intended to be carried on by the transferee company post-amalgamation, the amalgamation MUST be accounted for as:
A. Amalgamation in the nature of Merger
B. Amalgamation in the nature of Purchase ✔
C. Pooling of Interests Method
D. Reconstruction in the nature of Merger
Explanation: One of the 5 essential conditions for an amalgamation in the nature of merger under AS 14 is that the business of the transferor company is intended to be carried on by the transferee company. If this condition is violated, it is classified as an amalgamation in the nature of purchase.
Medium NORMAL · Transferor Company Books | Settlement of Preference Shareholders | Journal Entries
In the books of the Transferor Company, how are preference shareholders' claims settled when shares of the Transferee Company are received specifically for them as part of Purchase Consideration?
A. Debited to Realisation A/c and Credited to Transferee Co. Shares A/c
B. Debited to Preference Shareholders A/c and Credited to Shares in Transferee Co. A/c ✔
C. Debited to Equity Shareholders A/c and Credited to Preference Shareholders A/c
D. Debited to Bank A/c and Credited to Preference Share Capital A/c
Explanation: When shares in transferee company received for preference shareholders are distributed to them, the entry in the transferor company's books is: Preference Shareholders A/c Dr. To Shares in Transferee Company A/c.
Medium NORMAL · Statutory Reserves | AS 14 | Comparative Treatment
Which of the following statements is CORRECT regarding the treatment of statutory reserves under AS 14?
A. Statutory reserves are preserved only under the Pooling of Interests Method.
B. Statutory reserves are preserved under both Merger and Purchase methods, but under the Purchase method, an Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve account is used. ✔
C. Statutory reserves are written off to Profit and Loss Account upon amalgamation.
D. Statutory reserves under Purchase method are directly credited to Capital Reserve.
Explanation: Statutory reserves must be maintained by the transferee company as required by law. In merger (pooling of interests), all reserves are taken over naturally. In purchase method, statutory reserves are incorporated by debiting 'Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve Account' and crediting the relevant statutory reserve.
CASE SCENARIO: Vanguard Ltd acquires the entire business of Zenith Ltd on 1st April 2026. The Balance Sheet of Zenith Ltd as on 31st March 2026 shows: Equity Share Capital (1,00,000 shares of ₹10 each) ₹10,00,000; 12% Preference Share Capital (4,000 shares of ₹100 each) ₹4,00,000; General Reserve ₹3,00,000; Export Profit Reserve (Statutory Reserve) ₹1,00,000; Profit & Loss A/c (Cr.) ₹2,00,000; 10% Debentures ₹5,00,000; Trade Payables ₹2,00,000. Assets consist of: Property, Plant & Equipment ₹18,00,000; Inventory ₹4,00,000; Trade Receivables ₹3,50,000; Cash at Bank ₹1,50,000. Vanguard Ltd agreed to: (1) Issue 3 Equity Shares of ₹10 each (agreed value ₹15 per share) for every 2 Equity Shares in Zenith Ltd. (2) Issue 11% Preference Shares of ₹100 each at par to redeem the 12% Preference Shareholders of Zenith Ltd at a premium of 10%. (3) Discharge 10% Debentures of Zenith Ltd at a 5% premium by issuing 12% Debentures of Vanguard Ltd at par. (4) Expenses of liquidation of ₹30,000 were paid by Vanguard Ltd. The amalgamation is in the nature of purchase. Export Profit Reserve is to be maintained for 2 more years.
Medium SCENARIO · Purchase Consideration | Net Payment Method | AS 14
Calculate the total Purchase Consideration for Zenith Ltd as per AS 14.
A. ₹26,90,000
B. ₹22,50,000
C. ₹26,40,000 ✔
D. ₹31,90,000
Explanation: Purchase consideration is aggregate payment to shareholders. (1) Equity Shareholders: (1,00,000 / 2) * 3 = 1,50,000 shares * ₹15 = ₹22,50,000. (2) Preference Shareholders: ₹4,00,000 + 10% premium = ₹4,40,000. Total PC = ₹22,50,000 + ₹4,40,000 = ₹26,40,000. (Debenture discharge is not part of PC).
Hard SCENARIO · Net Assets Taken Over | Liabilities Assumed | Debenture Settlement
Compute the Net Agreed Assets taken over by Vanguard Ltd (excluding goodwill/capital reserve calculation).
A. ₹20,00,000
B. ₹19,75,000 ✔
C. ₹27,00,000
D. ₹21,75,000
Explanation: Total Assets taken over = PPE (₹18,00,000) + Inventory (₹4,00,000) + Debtors (₹3,50,000) + Bank (₹1,50,000) = ₹27,00,000. Liabilities assumed = Trade Payables (₹2,00,000) + 10% Debentures discharge value (₹5,00,000 * 1.05 = ₹5,25,000) = ₹7,25,000. Net Assets taken over = ₹27,00,000 - ₹7,25,000 = ₹19,75,000.
Hard SCENARIO · Goodwill | Liquidation Expenses | Purchase Method
What is the amount of Goodwill / Capital Reserve arising on acquisition (after considering liquidation expenses paid by Vanguard Ltd)?
A. Goodwill of ₹6,95,000 ✔
B. Capital Reserve of ₹6,65,000
C. Goodwill of ₹6,65,000
D. Goodwill of ₹6,35,000
Explanation: Excess of PC over Net Assets = ₹26,40,000 - ₹19,75,000 = ₹6,65,000 (Goodwill). Liquidation expenses of ₹30,000 paid by transferee under purchase method are debited to Goodwill Account. Total Goodwill = ₹6,65,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹6,95,000.
Medium SCENARIO · Statutory Reserve | Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve | Purchase Method
How is Export Profit Reserve recorded in Vanguard Ltd's books?
A. Debited to General Reserve A/c ₹1,00,000 and Credited to Export Profit Reserve A/c ₹1,00,000
B. Debited to Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c ₹1,00,000 and Credited to Export Profit Reserve A/c ₹1,00,000 ✔
C. Debited to Goodwill A/c ₹1,00,000 and Credited to Export Profit Reserve A/c ₹1,00,000
D. No entry is made because it is a statutory reserve under purchase method.
Explanation: Under the purchase method, to maintain statutory reserve, Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve Account is debited and Export Profit Reserve Account is credited with ₹1,00,000.
CASE SCENARIO: Titan Ltd and Orion Ltd decide to amalgamate to form a new company, Nova Ltd, on 1st April 2026. The amalgamation satisfies all 5 conditions of an 'amalgamation in the nature of merger' under AS 14. Balance Sheet summaries as on 31st March 2026: - Titan Ltd: Equity Share Capital (₹10 each) ₹20,00,000; General Reserve ₹5,00,000; Profit & Loss A/c ₹3,00,000; Liabilities ₹4,00,000. Total Assets ₹32,00,000. - Orion Ltd: Equity Share Capital (₹10 each) ₹10,00,000; General Reserve ₹2,00,000; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory) ₹1,00,000; Profit & Loss A/c ₹1,00,000; Liabilities ₹2,00,000. Total Assets ₹16,00,000. Nova Ltd issues equity shares of ₹10 each fully paid to the equity shareholders of both companies to satisfy the purchase consideration. Total PC paid: To Titan Ltd = ₹22,00,000 in shares; To Orion Ltd = ₹11,00,000 in shares.
Hard SCENARIO · Pooling of Interests Method | General Reserve Adjustment | Merger
Under the Pooling of Interests Method, what is the balance of General Reserve of Nova Ltd immediately after amalgamation (before any other adjustments)?
A. ₹7,00,000
B. ₹4,00,000 ✔
C. ₹5,00,000
D. Nil
Explanation: Combined General Reserves of transferors = ₹5,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹7,00,000. Adjustment for excess PC over face value of share capital: Titan Ltd PC excess = ₹22,00,000 - ₹20,00,000 = ₹2,00,000. Orion Ltd PC excess = ₹11,00,000 - ₹10,00,000 = ₹1,00,000. Total excess PC = ₹3,00,000. Net General Reserve = ₹7,00,000 - ₹3,00,000 = ₹4,00,000.
Medium SCENARIO · Pooling of Interests Method | Statutory Reserves | Direct Incorporation
How is the Investment Allowance Reserve of Orion Ltd incorporated in Nova Ltd's books?
A. Debited to Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve A/c and credited to Investment Allowance Reserve A/c
B. Incorporated directly as Investment Allowance Reserve A/c ₹1,00,000 without using Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve ✔
C. Transferred to Capital Reserve A/c
D. Ignored since it belongs to the transferor company
Explanation: Under the Pooling of Interests Method (merger), all reserves (including statutory reserves) are taken over directly at book values into the respective reserve accounts. Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve account is NOT used in merger accounting.
Easy SCENARIO · Pooling of Interests Method | Profit and Loss Preservation | Merger
What is the total Profit & Loss Account balance appearing in the balance sheet of Nova Ltd post-amalgamation?
A. ₹4,00,000 ✔
B. ₹3,00,000
C. ₹1,00,000
D. Nil
Explanation: Under the pooling of interests method, the profit and loss account balances of transferor companies are preserved and combined: ₹3,00,000 (Titan) + ₹1,00,000 (Orion) = ₹4,00,000.
Easy SCENARIO · Share Capital Issued | Purchase Consideration | Nova Ltd
What is the total Paid-up Equity Share Capital of Nova Ltd after issuing shares for amalgamation?
A. ₹30,00,000
B. ₹33,00,000 ✔
C. ₹48,00,000
D. ₹32,00,000
Explanation: Nova Ltd issued shares of face value ₹10 each for total purchase consideration: ₹22,00,000 (for Titan Ltd) + ₹11,00,000 (for Orion Ltd) = ₹33,00,000.
CASE SCENARIO: Kavya Ltd and Navya Ltd operate in the same industry. Kavya Ltd agrees to absorb Navya Ltd on 31st March 2026. The intrinsic value per share of Kavya Ltd is ₹40 (face value ₹10) and Navya Ltd is ₹20 (face value ₹10). Navya Ltd's Share Capital consists of 80,000 equity shares of ₹10 each fully paid. Additional Facts: 1. Consideration is to be discharged on the basis of Intrinsic Value ratio by issuing fully paid Equity Shares of Kavya Ltd. 2. Cash is to be paid for any fractional share entitlements. 3. Navya Ltd has 1,00,000 trade payables, including ₹20,00,000 due to Kavya Ltd. 4. Unsold inventory of Kavya Ltd includes goods purchased from Navya Ltd for ₹6,00,000 on which Navya Ltd made a profit of 20% on cost.
Medium SCENARIO · Intrinsic Value Method | Exchange Ratio | Share Computation
Calculate the share exchange ratio and total number of full equity shares to be issued by Kavya Ltd to Navya Ltd shareholders.
A. 1 share of Kavya for every 2 shares of Navya; 40,000 shares ✔
B. 2 shares of Kavya for every 1 share of Navya; 1,60,000 shares
C. 1 share of Kavya for every 4 shares of Navya; 20,000 shares
D. 3 shares of Kavya for every 4 shares of Navya; 60,000 shares
Explanation: Exchange ratio = Intrinsic Value of Navya / Intrinsic Value of Kavya = ₹20 / ₹40 = 0.5 (1 share of Kavya for every 2 shares of Navya). Total shares to be issued = 80,000 * 0.5 = 40,000 equity shares.
Medium SCENARIO · Purchase Consideration | Intrinsic Value | Valuation
What is the total Purchase Consideration under AS 14 (assuming no fractional shares)?
A. ₹8,00,000
B. ₹16,00,000 ✔
C. ₹20,00,000
D. ₹32,00,000
Explanation: Total PC = Number of shares issued (40,000) * Agreed Intrinsic Value / Issue Price per share of Kavya Ltd (₹40) = 40,000 * ₹40 = ₹16,00,000.
Medium SCENARIO · Unrealized Profit | Inter-company Stock | Inventory Adjustment
What is the amount of unrealized profit included in inventory to be adjusted post-absorption?
A. ₹1,20,000
B. ₹1,00,000 ✔
C. ₹60,00,000
D. ₹80,000
Explanation: Profit element on cost = 20%. Selling price = Cost + 20% = 120%. Profit included in invoice value of ₹6,00,000 = ₹6,00,000 * (20 / 120) = ₹1,00,000.
Easy SCENARIO · Mutual Owings | Inter-company Balances | Cancellation
What entry is passed in Kavya Ltd's books to eliminate mutual owing/trade payables post-amalgamation?
A. Trade Payables A/c Dr. ₹20,00,000 To Trade Receivables A/c ₹20,00,000 ✔
B. Trade Receivables A/c Dr. ₹20,00,000 To Trade Payables A/c ₹20,00,000
C. Trade Payables A/c Dr. ₹1,00,000 To Trade Receivables A/c ₹1,00,000
D. Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹20,00,000 To Trade Receivables A/c ₹20,00,000
Explanation: To eliminate the mutual balance between Kavya Ltd and Navya Ltd of ₹20,00,000, Trade Payables Account is debited and Trade Receivables Account is credited with ₹20,00,000.
CASE SCENARIO: Apex Ltd absorbs Zenith Ltd on 1st April 2026 under the purchase method. Balance Sheet details of Zenith Ltd on 31st March 2026: - Equity Share Capital (50,00,000 shares of ₹10 each) = ₹500 lakhs - 10% Preference Share Capital = ₹100 lakhs - General Reserve = ₹200 lakhs - Statutory Reserve = ₹50 lakhs - Profit & Loss A/c (Dr. balance) = ₹(40) lakhs - Non-Current Liabilities = ₹300 lakhs - Current Liabilities = ₹140 lakhs - Total Assets (Book Value) = ₹1,210 lakhs Agreed Valuation Terms: 1. Non-Current Assets (book value ₹800 lakhs) valued at ₹900 lakhs. 2. Current Assets (book value ₹410 lakhs) valued at ₹380 lakhs. 3. Apex Ltd issues 4 equity shares of ₹10 each (market price ₹25) for every 5 equity shares of Zenith Ltd. 4. Preference shareholders are paid at 10% premium in cash. 5. Non-current liabilities are taken over at book value.
Hard SCENARIO · Purchase Consideration | Net Payment Method | Calculation
What is the Purchase Consideration payable by Apex Ltd under AS 14?
A. ₹1,000 lakhs
B. ₹1,110 lakhs ✔
C. ₹1,010 lakhs
D. ₹1,210 lakhs
