Explanation: As per the proviso to section 6(1)(c), for an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India whose total income (other than income from foreign sources) does not exceed Rs. 15 lakhs, the period of 60 days is substituted by 120 days.
Medium NORMAL · PIO | Indian Citizen | Visit to India | Income Threshold
What is the threshold limit of total income (other than income from foreign sources) under Explanation 1(b) to section 6(1) for an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India, above which the 60-day period is substituted by 182 days instead of 120 days?
A. Rs. 10 lakhs
B. Rs. 15 lakhs ✔
C. Rs. 50 lakhs
D. Rs. 1 crore
Explanation: If the total income (other than income from foreign sources) of an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India exceeds Rs. 15 lakhs during the previous year, the 60-day period is substituted by 182 days.
Hard NORMAL · Residential Status | Indian Citizen | Non-Resident
An Indian citizen having total income (other than income from foreign sources) of Rs. 18 lakhs comes on a visit to India during the previous year 2025-26 and stays for 150 days. His residential status for AY 2026-27 is:
A. Resident and Ordinarily Resident
B. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident
C. Non-Resident ✔
D. Deemed Resident
Explanation: Since his total income (excluding foreign sources) exceeds Rs. 15 lakhs, the exception rule for visiting India does not apply the 120-day threshold; instead, the 182-day rule applies. Since his stay is 150 days (less than 182 days), he fails the basic conditions and is a Non-Resident.
Hard NORMAL · Deemed Resident | Section 6(1A) | Stateless Persons
What is a 'deemed resident' under section 6(1A)?
A. An individual who is a citizen of India, having total income (other than foreign sources) exceeding Rs. 15 lakhs, and who is not liable to tax in any other country or territory by reason of his domicile or residence. ✔
B. Any foreign citizen who stays in India for 182 days or more.
C. An Indian citizen who resides abroad for more than 182 days.
D. A company incorporated in India with foreign management.
Explanation: Section 6(1A) states that an individual being a citizen of India, having total income (other than income from foreign sources) exceeding Rs. 15 lakhs during the previous year, shall be deemed to be resident in India in that previous year, if he is not liable to tax in any other country or territory by reason of his domicile or residence or any other criteria of similar nature.
Medium NORMAL · Deemed Resident | RNOR | Section 6(6)
An individual who is deemed to be resident in India under section 6(1A) is always classified for that previous year as:
A. Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR)
B. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) ✔
C. Non-Resident (NR)
D. Either ROR or RNOR depending on past history
Explanation: As per the proviso to section 6(6), an individual who is deemed to be resident in India under section 6(1A) shall be treated as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) in India.
Easy NORMAL · ROR | Additional Conditions | Section 6(6)
To be classified as 'Resident and Ordinarily Resident' (ROR) in India, an individual must satisfy:
A. Only any one of the basic conditions under section 6(1)
B. Both the additional conditions under section 6(6) in addition to satisfying at least one basic condition ✔
C. Only the additional conditions without satisfying any basic condition
D. Both basic conditions and all four additional conditions
Explanation: An individual is Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) if he is a resident under section 6(1) and also satisfies both the additional conditions specified under section 6(6) (i.e., resident in 2 out of 10 preceding previous years and stay of 730 days or more in 7 preceding previous years).
Medium NORMAL · Additional Conditions | Section 6(6) | Distractor
Which of the following is NOT an additional condition under section 6(6) for determining whether an individual is Ordinarily Resident?
A. Resident in India in at least 2 out of 10 previous years preceding the relevant previous year
B. Present in India for 730 days or more during the 7 previous years preceding the relevant previous year
C. Present in India for 365 days or more during the 4 previous years preceding the relevant previous year ✔
D. He is not a deemed resident under section 6(1A)
Explanation: Option C mentions '365 days or more during 4 previous years', whereas the actual requirement under section 6(6)(a) is 730 days or more during the 7 preceding previous years. Thus, option C is incorrect and represents a distractor.
Easy NORMAL · HUF | Residential Status | Control and Management
An individual is a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF). When is the HUF considered a 'Resident' in India?
A. If the Karta is an Indian citizen
B. If the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India ✔
C. If all the coparceners reside in India for at least 182 days
D. If its turnover exceeds Rs. 50 crores in India
Explanation: Under section 6(2), an HUF is resident in India if the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India during the previous year.
Medium NORMAL · HUF | ROR | Section 6(6)
An HUF is considered 'Resident and Ordinarily Resident' (ROR) in India if its Karta or manager satisfies:
A. Both additional conditions under section 6(6)(b) (resident in 2 out of 10 years and 730+ days in 7 years) ✔
B. Only the basic conditions under section 6(1)
C. The control and management is wholly in India
D. The family has been in existence for over 5 years
Explanation: An HUF is ROR in India if its Karta or manager satisfies both the additional conditions under section 6(6)(b), i.e., he has been resident in India in at least 2 out of 10 preceding previous years and has been present in India for 730 days or more during the 7 preceding previous years.
Easy NORMAL · Company | POEM | Section 6(3)
A company is said to be resident in India in any previous year if:
A. It is an Indian company, OR its Place of Effective Management (POEM) in that year is in India ✔
B. It is registered under the Companies Act, 2013 only
C. Its entire shareholding is held by Indian residents
D. Its registered office is outside India but board meetings are held in India
Explanation: Under section 6(3), a company is resident in India if it is an Indian company, or if its Place of Effective Management (POEM) in that year is in India.
Medium NORMAL · POEM | Definition | Company
What is meant by 'Place of Effective Management' (POEM) for a company?
A. The place where the annual general meeting is held
B. The place where key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of business of an entity as a whole are, in substance made ✔
C. The place where the statutory audit is conducted
D. The place where the company's manufacturing plant is located
Explanation: POEM is defined as a place where key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of the business of an entity as a whole are in substance made.
Easy NORMAL · Firm | AOP | BOI | Control and Management
A Firm, AOP, or BOI is resident in India if:
A. Control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India ✔
B. Control and management is situated wholly outside India
C. All partners/members are resident in India
D. At least 50% of the profits arise in India
Explanation: Under section 6(2), a partnership firm, AOP, or BOI is resident in India if the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly or partly in India during the previous year. It is non-resident only if control and management is wholly outside India.
Medium NORMAL · Residential Status | Foreign Company | Non-Resident
Which of the following persons is always considered 'Non-Resident' in India, regardless of their management location?
A. Foreign Institutional Investor
B. Local Authority
C. None of the above (Every person other than an individual/HUF/Company can be resident if control is in India)
D. Foreign Company with POEM outside India ✔
Explanation: A foreign company whose POEM is outside India is always non-resident. For local authorities and artificial juridical persons, residency depends on whether control and management is situated wholly or partly in India.
Easy NORMAL · Scope of Total Income | ROR | Section 5(1)
For a 'Resident and Ordinarily Resident' (ROR) individual, the scope of total income under section 5(1) includes:
A. Income received or deemed to be received in India + Income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India + Income accruing or arising outside India ✔
B. Only income received in India
C. Only Indian income
D. Income received in India and income accruing in India from a business controlled from India
Explanation: The total income of an ROR includes all incomes from all sources, whether received, accruing, or arising inside or outside India, as per section 5(1).
Hard NORMAL · Scope of Total Income | RNOR | Section 5(1)
For a 'Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident' (RNOR) individual, which of the following incomes is taxable in India?
A. Income accruing or arising outside India from a business controlled from outside India
B. Income accruing or arising outside India from a business controlled from or set up in India ✔
C. Only foreign income remitted to India
D. Income from any source outside India
Explanation: Under section 5(1), for an RNOR, income accruing or arising outside India is taxable only if it is derived from a business controlled from or set up in India.
Easy NORMAL · Scope of Total Income | Non-Resident | Section 5(2)
For a Non-Resident (NR) individual, the scope of total income under section 5(2) includes:
A. Only income received or deemed to be received in India AND income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India ✔
B. All global incomes
C. Income received in India plus foreign business income
D. Income remitted to India during the previous year
Explanation: As per section 5(2), a Non-Resident is taxable in India only for Indian income—meaning income received/deemed received in India and income accruing/arising/deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Hard NORMAL · Scope of Total Income | RNOR | Business Controlled from India
Income earned and received outside India from a foreign business controlled from India is taxable in the hands of:
A. ROR only
B. ROR and RNOR ✔
C. ROR, RNOR, and Non-Resident
D. None of the persons
Explanation: Foreign income from a business controlled from India is taxable for both ROR and RNOR, but NOT for a Non-Resident.
Medium NORMAL · Deemed to Accrue or Arise | Section 9 | Business Connection
Which of the following incomes is deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9?
A. Income from any business connection in India ✔
B. Salary earned for service rendered outside India to an Indian citizen by a foreign employer
C. Dividend paid by a foreign company outside India to an Indian resident
D. Interest paid by a non-resident on a foreign currency loan utilized outside India
Explanation: Under section 9(1)(i), all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India, or through or from any property in India, is deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Medium NORMAL · Salary | Government Employee | Section 9(1)(iii)
Salary payable by the Government of India to an Indian citizen for services rendered outside India is:
A. Exempt from tax
B. Deemed to accrue or arise in India ✔
C. Taxable only if remitted to India
D. Taxable only if the citizen is ROR
Explanation: Under section 9(1)(iii), salary payable by the Government to a citizen of India for services rendered outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India. (Note: Allowances and perquisites are exempt under section 10(7)).
Medium NORMAL · Dividend | Indian Company | Section 9(1)(iv)
Dividend paid by an Indian company outside India is:
A. Deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(iv) ✔
B. Exempt under section 10(34)
C. Taxable only in the hands of Non-Residents
D. Exempt in all cases
Explanation: Under section 9(1)(iv), dividend paid by an Indian company outside India is deemed to accrue or arise in India and is taxable.
Hard NORMAL · Interest | Non-Resident Borrower | Section 9(1)(v)
Interest paid by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India if the borrowed moneys are:
A. Used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by him in India ✔
B. Utilized outside India for personal investments
C. Deposited in a foreign bank account
D. Used to pay taxes in a foreign country
Explanation: Under section 9(1)(v)(b), interest payable by a non-resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India if the borrowed moneys are used for the purposes of a business or profession carried on by him in India.
Hard NORMAL · Royalty | Section 9(1)(vi) | Exception
Royalty payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India EXCEPT when the royalty is payable in respect of any right, property, or information used for:
A. A business or profession carried on by the resident outside India or for the purpose of making or earning any income from any source outside India ✔
B. A business carried on in India
C. Manufacturing goods sold within India
D. Providing services to Indian residents
Explanation: Under section 9(1)(vi), royalty payable by a resident is deemed to accrue or arise in India unless it is payable in respect of a right, property, or information used for a business or profession carried on outside India or to earn income from outside India.
Medium NORMAL · Fees for Technical Services | Government | Section 9(1)(vii)
Fees for technical services (FTS) payable by the Central Government or State Government is deemed to accrue or arise in India:
A. Always, regardless of where the services are utilized ✔
B. Only if services are utilized in India
C. Only if the recipient is an Indian citizen
D. Never
Explanation: Under section 9(1)(vii), FTS payable by the Central or State Government is deemed to accrue or arise in India in all cases, even if the services are utilized outside India.
Easy NORMAL · Scope of Total Income | General Principle | Single Taxation
Where an income is received in India and also accrues in India, how many times is it included in total income?
A. Twice
B. Once ✔
C. Three times
D. It is ignored
Explanation: An income is included in total income only once, even if it is both received in India and accrues in India. Double taxation of the same receipt in the same assessment year for the same person is not permitted.
Medium NORMAL · Remittance | Past Foreign Income | Receipt Basis
Remittance of past untaxed foreign income into India in the current previous year is:
A. Taxable as income of the current previous year
B. Not taxable in the current previous year because it was already income of a past year ✔
C. Taxable only for ROR
D. Taxable as capital gains
Explanation: Remittance of past foreign income to India does not result in taxable income in the year of remittance, as income is taxable on receipt or accrual basis (whichever is earlier). Once accrued outside India in a past year, bringing it to India later is merely a remittance of capital/wealth.
Hard NORMAL · SEP | Significant Economic Presence | Section 9(1)(i)
Which of the following provisions deals with the taxability of 'Significant Economic Presence' (SEP) in India for non-residents?
A. Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) ✔
B. Section 6(3)
C. Section 5(2)
D. Section 9(1)(vii)
Explanation: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) introduces the concept of Significant Economic Presence (SEP), which constitutes a business connection in India for non-residents based on transactions or user/download thresholds.
Easy NORMAL · Residential Status | Previous Year | General Rule
If a person is a resident in India in respect of the previous year 2025-26, his status for the assessment year 2026-27 is determined for:
A. The entire financial year 2025-26 ✔
B. Only the period during which he stayed in India
C. The assessment year 2026-27
D. The preceding 4 financial years
Explanation: Residential status is determined for each previous year as a whole. A person is either resident or non-resident for the entire previous year; there is no split-year residency under general Indian tax law.
Hard NORMAL · CDC | Ship Crew | Exclusion of Days
An Indian ship's crew member leaves India on a voyage. For computing his period of stay in India under section 6(1), the period beginning on the date entered into the Continuous Discharge Certificate (CDC) and ending on the date entered therein as co-terminating with the voyage shall:
A. Be excluded from his stay in India ✔
B. Be included as his stay in India
C. Be counted as double stay
D. Be ignored unless he is an Indian citizen
Explanation: As per Explanation 2 to section 6(1), in the case of an individual, being a citizen of India and a member of the crew of an Indian ship, the period beginning on the date entered into the CDC and ending on the date of termination shall not be included in computing his stay in India.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Raghav, an Indian citizen, left India for the first time on 15th October 2025 for taking up employment in Germany. During the financial year 2025-26, his total income from Indian sources is Rs. 12 lakhs, and his foreign-source income is Rs. 8 lakhs. He has been residing in India all his life prior to this financial year.
Medium SCENARIO · Calculation of Stay | Departure Date | Employment Abroad
What is the number of days Mr. Raghav stayed in India during the previous year 2025-26?
A. 197 days
B. 198 days ✔
C. 196 days
D. 182 days
Explanation: From 1st April 2025 to 15th October 2025: April (30) + May (31) + June (30) + July (31) + August (31) + September (30) + October (15) = 198 days. Both arrival and departure dates are counted as days spent in India.
Medium SCENARIO · Employment Abroad | Basic Condition | Section 6(1)
Which basic condition is applicable to Mr. Raghav for the previous year 2025-26, considering he left India for employment?
A. He must be in India for 182 days or more, because the 60-day rule is replaced by 182 days for an Indian citizen leaving for employment. ✔
B. He must be in India for 60 days or more.
C. He must be in India for 120 days or more.
D. He is automatically a non-resident because he left India.
Explanation: Under the exception to section 6(1), an Indian citizen who leaves India during the previous year for employment outside India must satisfy the 182-day threshold instead of 60 days.
Hard SCENARIO · Residential Status | ROR | Employment Exception
What is the residential status of Mr. Raghav for the assessment year 2026-27?
A. Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) ✔
B. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR)
C. Non-Resident (NR)
D. Deemed Resident
Explanation: Mr. Raghav stayed in India for 198 days (exceeding 182 days), making him a resident. Since he resided in India all his life prior to this year, he satisfies both additional conditions under section 6(6), making him ROR.
Medium SCENARIO · Scope of Total Income | ROR | Global Income
How will Mr. Raghav's global income be taxed in India for AY 2026-27?
A. Only Indian income of Rs. 12 lakhs is taxable.
B. Both Indian income of Rs. 12 lakhs and foreign income of Rs. 8 lakhs are taxable in India. ✔
C. Only foreign income is taxable.
D. Neither Indian nor foreign income is taxable.
Explanation: Since Mr. Raghav is a Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) for AY 2026-27, his global income (both Indian and foreign source income) is taxable in India.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. John, a foreign citizen of non-Indian origin, comes to India for the first time on 1st June 2025. He stays in India continuously and leaves on 28th September 2025. During the previous year 2025-26, he does not visit India again. His total income from Indian business is Rs. 10 lakhs and foreign business is Rs. 25 lakhs.
Medium SCENARIO · Stay Calculation | Foreign Citizen | Days Count
Calculate the total number of days Mr. John stayed in India during the previous year 2025-26.
A. 120 days ✔
B. 119 days
C. 121 days
D. 118 days
Explanation: June (30) + July (31) + August (31) + September (28) = 120 days. Both the date of arrival (1st June) and date of departure (28th September) are included.
Hard SCENARIO · Non-Resident | Foreign Citizen | 182 Days Rule
What is the residential status of Mr. John for the assessment year 2026-27?
A. Resident and Ordinarily Resident
B. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident
C. Non-Resident ✔
D. Deemed Resident
Explanation: Mr. John stayed in India for 120 days. Since he is a foreign citizen of non-Indian origin, the basic condition of 182 days applies to him (the 120-day or 182-day visit rules for PIO/citizens do not apply to foreign citizens of non-Indian origin). Since 120 < 182, he is a Non-Resident.
Medium SCENARIO · Scope of Total Income | Non-Resident | Section 5(2)
Which of Mr. John's incomes are taxable in India for the assessment year 2026-27?
A. Only Indian business income of Rs. 10 lakhs ✔
B. Both Indian business income of Rs. 10 lakhs and foreign business income of Rs. 25 lakhs
C. Only foreign business income of Rs. 25 lakhs
D. Neither income is taxable in India
Explanation: Since Mr. John is a Non-Resident for AY 2026-27, only income received, accruing, or arising (or deemed so) in India is taxable. Thus, only Rs. 10 lakhs from Indian business is taxable.
Hard SCENARIO · PIO | 120 days rule | Income Threshold
Would Mr. John's status change if he was a person of Indian origin (PIO) visiting India under the same facts, assuming his foreign income is from foreign sources?
A. Yes, he would become a Resident since his stay of 120 days meets the relaxed condition for PIO visiting India with income not exceeding Rs. 15 lakhs. ✔
B. No, his status would remain Non-Resident.
C. He would automatically become a deemed resident.
D. He would become ROR immediately.
Explanation: For an Indian citizen or PIO visiting India whose total income (excl. foreign sources) does not exceed Rs. 15 lakhs, a stay of 120 days or more triggers residency under section 6(1)(c). Here his stay is exactly 120 days and Indian income is Rs. 10 lakhs (<= 15 lakhs), so he would be a resident.
CASE SCENARIO: M/s. Zenith Global Inc., a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, operates a digital platform providing cloud services. During the previous year 2025-26, it has significant transactions with users in India, exceeding the prescribed monetary threshold under Significant Economic Presence (SEP). Its Board of Directors holds all meetings in London, and its day-to-day management is also conducted from the UK.
Hard SCENARIO · Foreign Company | POEM | SEP vs Residence
What is the residential status of M/s. Zenith Global Inc. in India for the assessment year 2026-27?
A. Resident in India ✔
B. Non-Resident in India
C. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident
D. Deemed Indian Company
Explanation: Under section 6(3), a foreign company is resident in India if its Place of Effective Management (POEM) is in India. However, due to SEP under section 9(1)(i), its income is deemed to accrue or arise in India. Wait, does SEP make a company resident? No, SEP only creates a business connection (taxability of income), not residential status. Since its POEM is in the UK, it is a Non-Resident company.
Hard SCENARIO · SEP | Business Connection | Section 9(1)(i)
How is the UK company taxed on its income derived from Indian users through SEP?
A. Taxable in India because SEP constitutes a business connection under section 9(1)(i). ✔
B. Not taxable in India because it is a non-resident company with POEM outside India.
C. Taxable only if the company remits the money to an Indian bank account.
D. Exempt under double taxation avoidance agreements unconditionally.
Explanation: Under Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i), Significant Economic Presence (SEP) constitutes a business connection in India. Therefore, income attributable to SEP is deemed to accrue or arise in India and is taxable even for a non-resident.
Medium SCENARIO · POEM | Foreign Company | Resident Company
If M/s. Zenith Global Inc. had its Place of Effective Management (POEM) located in Mumbai during the previous year 2025-26, what would be its residential status?
A. Resident in India ✔
B. Non-Resident in India
C. RNOR
D. Resident only for UK tax purposes
Explanation: As per section 6(3)(ii), a company other than an Indian company is resident in India if its Place of Effective Management (POEM) in that year is in India.
Medium SCENARIO · Company | ROR / RNOR | Categories of Residence
Can a foreign company be classified as 'Resident and Ordinarily Resident' or 'Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident'?
A. No, companies are classified only as Resident or Non-Resident. ✔
B. Yes, foreign companies can be RNOR.
C. Yes, if their Karta is resident in India.
D. Only if they have branches in India.
Explanation: The categories of ROR and RNOR apply only to individuals and Hindu Undivided Families (HUF). Companies and other persons are classified strictly as either Resident or Non-Resident.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Dev, an Indian citizen and a successful consultant, has been living in Dubai for the past 12 years. For the previous year 2025-26, his total income from Indian sources (business and capital gains) is Rs. 22 lakhs, and his income from Dubai sources is Rs. 40 lakhs. In Dubai, Mr. Dev is not liable to pay any personal income tax due to local tax laws. During 2025-26, he visited India for 110 days.
Hard SCENARIO · Indian Citizen | Visit to India | 182 days rule
What is Mr. Dev's residential status in India for AY 2026-27 under the normal basic conditions?
A. Resident, because his stay is 110 days and income exceeds Rs. 15 lakhs.
B. Non-Resident, because his stay of 110 days is less than 182 days and also less than the 120-day threshold for a visiting PIO/Indian citizen. ✔
C. Resident and Ordinarily Resident
D. Resident because he is an Indian citizen abroad.
Explanation: Mr. Dev is an Indian citizen visiting India with Indian income > Rs. 15 lakhs. For such persons, the threshold is 182 days (since income > 15 lakhs). His stay is 110 days (< 182 days), so he fails the basic condition under section 6(1).
Hard SCENARIO · Deemed Resident | Section 6(1A) | Stateless Tax Resident
Is Mr. Dev covered by the 'deemed resident' provision under section 6(1A)?
A. Yes, because he is an Indian citizen, his Indian-source income exceeds Rs. 15 lakhs, and he is not liable to tax in Dubai. ✔
B. No, because he is a non-resident under section 6(1).
C. No, because he stayed for less than 182 days in India.
D. Yes, because he lived in Dubai for 12 years.
Explanation: Section 6(1A) applies to an Indian citizen whose total income (excl. foreign sources) exceeds Rs. 15 lakhs, and who is not liable to tax in any other country by reason of domicile/residence. All these conditions are met by Mr. Dev.
Medium SCENARIO · Deemed Resident | RNOR | Proviso to Section 6(6)
What is the specific residential status assigned to Mr. Dev by virtue of being a 'deemed resident' under section 6(1A)?
A. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) ✔
B. Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR)
C. Non-Resident (NR)
D. Deemed Non-Resident
Explanation: As per the proviso to section 6(6), an individual who is deemed to be resident in India under section 6(1A) shall be treated as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) in India for that previous year.
Hard SCENARIO · RNOR | Foreign Income | Taxability
What will be the taxability of Mr. Dev's Dubai income of Rs. 40 lakhs in India for AY 2026-27?
A. Not taxable in India, because an RNOR is not taxable on foreign income unless it is from a business controlled from or set up in India. ✔
B. Taxable in India in full because he is a deemed resident.
C. Taxable only if remitted to India.
D. Taxable at special flat rate of 20%.
Explanation: Since Mr. Dev is an RNOR (due to being a deemed resident under section 6(1A)), his foreign-source income (Dubai income of Rs. 40 lakhs) is not taxable in India unless it is from a business controlled from or set up in India (which is not the case here). Only Indian income of Rs. 22 lakhs is taxable.
CASE SCENARIO: A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) has its Karta, Mr. Rajesh, residing permanently in Singapore. The control and management of the HUF's affairs is partially exercised from Delhi by a committee of senior members, and partially from Singapore by Mr. Rajesh. Mr. Rajesh has been visiting India for past many years and satisfies both additional conditions of section 6(6).
Medium SCENARIO · HUF | Control and Management | Resident HUF
What is the residential status of the HUF in India for the previous year?
A. Resident in India ✔
B. Non-Resident in India
C. Deemed Resident
D. Resident only in Singapore
Explanation: Under section 6(2), an HUF is resident in India if the control and management of its affairs is situated *wholly or partly* in India. Since part of the control is exercised from Delhi, the HUF is a resident in India.
Medium SCENARIO · HUF | ROR | Karta
What is the category of residency (ROR or RNOR) for the HUF?
A. Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) ✔
B. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR)
C. Non-Resident
D. Neither ROR nor RNOR
Explanation: An HUF is ROR in India if its Karta or manager satisfies both additional conditions under section 6(6)(b). Since Mr. Rajesh satisfies both additional conditions, the HUF is Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR).
Medium SCENARIO · HUF | RNOR | Section 6(6)(b)
If Mr. Rajesh (the Karta) did NOT satisfy the additional conditions under section 6(6)(b), what would be the residential status category of the HUF?
A. Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR) ✔
B. Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR)
C. Non-Resident
D. Deemed Resident
Explanation: If the Karta or manager of a resident HUF does not satisfy both additional conditions, the HUF is classified as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR).
Easy SCENARIO · HUF | Global Income | ROR Scope
Which of the following incomes will be included in the total income of the HUF if it is assessed as ROR?
A. Only Indian income
B. Global income (both Indian and foreign income from all sources) ✔
C. Only income controlled from Delhi
D. Only remittances made to India
Explanation: An HUF that is Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) is taxable on its global income, exactly like an ROR individual.

Paper 3: Taxation · Module 2 · Chapter 4:

Taxation — 55 rows
Easy NORMAL · Transfer of Income | Section 60 | Clubbing of Income
Under section 60 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, if a person transfers the income from any asset without transferring the asset itself, such income shall be included in the total income of:
A. The transferee
B. The transferor ✔
C. Both jointly in the ratio of their taxable income
D. Neither; it is exempt from tax
Explanation: Section 60 deals with transfer of income without transfer of asset. It explicitly mandates that where a person transfers income from any asset without transferring the ownership of the asset, such income shall be included in the total income of the transferor.
Easy NORMAL · Revocable Transfer | Section 61 | House Property
Mr. A revokes a revocable transfer of a house property after 4 years in favor of his son. The income from the property before revocation will be taxed in the hands of:
A. Mr. A ✔
B. The son
C. Equally between Mr. A and the son
D. The HUF of Mr. A
Explanation: Under section 61, all income arising to any person by virtue of a revocable transfer of assets is taxable in the hands of the transferor (Mr. A).
Medium NORMAL · Revocable Transfer | Section 63 | Definitions
Which of the following transfers is considered an 'irrevocable transfer' for the purposes of income inclusion under sections 61 to 63?
A. A transfer which contains any provision for the re-transfer of the asset to the transferor at any time.
B. A transfer which gives the transferor a right to reassume power over the asset.
C. A transfer which is not revocable during the lifetime of the transferee. ✔
D. A transfer where the transferor can claim any income or asset back.
Explanation: Section 63 defines a revocable transfer as one containing any provision for re-transfer or right to reassume power. Conversely, a transfer not revocable during the lifetime of the beneficiary/transferee is treated as irrevocable (provided certain conditions are met).
Easy NORMAL · Transfer to Spouse | Section 64(1)(iv) | Inadequate Consideration
As per section 64(1)(iv), when an individual transfers an asset (other than house property) to their spouse for inadequate consideration, the income from such asset is included in the total income of:
A. The spouse
B. The individual transferor ✔
C. Both equally
D. The person who utilizes the asset
Explanation: Section 64(1)(iv) provides that income from assets transferred directly or indirectly to the spouse otherwise than for adequate consideration or in connection with an agreement to live apart is clubbed in the total income of the individual transferor.
Medium NORMAL · Accretion of Income | Section 64(1)(iv) | Clubbing
Mr. X transfers 10,000 shares of a company to his wife Mrs. X as a gift. Mrs. X receives a dividend of Rs. 50,000. Mrs. X invests this dividend and earns interest of Rs. 5,000. How much amount will be clubbed in the income of Mr. X?
A. Rs. 55,000
B. Rs. 50,000 ✔
C. Rs. 45,000
D. Nil
Explanation: Under section 64(1)(iv), only the direct income from the transferred asset (dividend of Rs. 50,000) is clubbed. Income from accretion or reinvestment of such income (interest of Rs. 5,000) is not clubbed in the hands of the transferor.
Medium NORMAL · Deemed Owner | House Property | Section 27 | Section 64
If an individual transfers a house property to their spouse for inadequate consideration, who is deemed to be the owner of the house property for tax purposes under section 27, and how is the income taxed?
A. Spouse is owner; income is taxed in hands of spouse.
B. Transferor is deemed owner; income is taxed in hands of transferor under clubbing provisions. ✔
C. Both are co-owners in 50:50 ratio.
D. The income is exempt under section 10.
Explanation: Section 27(i) deems the transferor to be the owner of house property transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration. Consequently, the income is computed in the hands of the transferor and clubbed under section 64.
Easy NORMAL · Daughter-in-law | Section 64(1)(vi) | Clubbing
Mr. B transfers cash to his son’s wife (daughter-in-law) for inadequate consideration. The income earned by the daughter-in-law from such cash will be clubbed in the total income of:
A. Mr. B ✔
B. Mr. B’s son
C. The daughter-in-law herself
D. Mr. B’s HUF
Explanation: Section 64(1)(vi) states that income from assets transferred directly or indirectly to a daughter-in-law otherwise than for adequate consideration is included in the total income of the transferor (Mr. B).
Medium NORMAL · Trust Benefit | Section 64(1)(viii) | Daughter-in-law
Mr. C transfers securities to a trust, and the income from the trust is applied for the immediate benefit of his son’s wife for inadequate consideration. Such income shall be clubbed with the income of:
A. The trust
B. Mr. C ✔
C. The son
D. The son's wife
Explanation: Under section 64(1)(viii), income arising directly or indirectly from assets transferred directly or indirectly to any person or association of persons for the immediate or deferred benefit of the transferor's son's wife, otherwise than for adequate consideration, is clubbed in the hands of the transferor.
Easy NORMAL · Minor Child Income | Section 64(1A) | Exceptions
Which of the following incomes of a minor child is NOT included in the total income of the parent under section 64(1A)?
A. Income earned from manual work. ✔
B. Income earned from fixed deposits made out of gift from grandfather.
C. Interest income from a savings bank account opened with gift money from mother.
D. Capital gains arising from sale of shares gifted by father.
Explanation: Section 64(1A) excludes income earned by a minor child from any manual work or from any activity involving application of their specialized skill, talent, or specialized knowledge and experience.
Easy NORMAL · Minor Child | Higher Income Parent | Section 64(1A)
If both parents are alive, in whose total income shall the income of a minor child be included under section 64(1A)?
A. Always the mother
B. Always the father
C. The parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher ✔
D. Equally divided between both parents
Explanation: Section 64(1A) prescribes that the income of a minor child shall be included in the total income of the parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher.
Easy NORMAL · Section 10(32) | Minor Exemption | Clubbing Limit
Once the income of a minor child is clubbed in the total income of a parent, what exemption is available to the parent under section 10(32)?
A. Full exemption of the minor's income
B. Exemption up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child ✔
C. Exemption up to Rs. 5,000 per minor child
D. No exemption is available
Explanation: Section 10(32) provides an exemption of up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child whose income is clubbed under section 64(1A), or the actual income clubbed, whichever is less.
Medium NORMAL · Disability | Section 80U | Minor Child Exception
How is the income of a minor child who suffers from any disability specified under section 80U treated for clubbing purposes?
A. It is clubbed in the parent's income as normal.
B. It is completely exempt from tax under section 10.
C. It is assessed directly in the hands of the minor child and is not clubbed in the parent's income. ✔
D. It is taxed at a flat rate of 10% in the hands of the guardian.
Explanation: As per the proviso to section 64(1A), the income of a minor child suffering from any disability of the nature specified in section 80U shall not be clubbed in the income of the parent, but shall be taxable in the hands of the minor child.
Medium NORMAL · Substantial Interest | Section 64(1)(ii) | Spouse Salary
Mr. D is a partner in a firm. His wife is employed in the same firm without any professional qualifications, and she draws a salary of Rs. 6,00,000. How will this salary be taxed?
A. Taxed entirely in the hands of the wife.
B. Included in the total income of Mr. D because he has a substantial interest in the firm. ✔
C. Divided equally between Mr. D and his wife.
D. Disallowed as an expense to the firm and tax-free for the wife.
Explanation: Under section 64(1)(ii), if a spouse of an individual having a substantial interest in a concern receives salary, commission, etc., from that concern without possessing technical or professional qualifications, such income is clubbed in the total income of the individual.
Medium NORMAL · Substantial Interest | Definition | Section 64
For the purpose of section 64(1)(ii) relating to remuneration of a spouse, what constitutes a 'substantial interest' in a company?
A. Beneficial ownership of shares carrying at least 10% of the voting power at any time during the previous year. ✔
B. Beneficial ownership of shares carrying at least 20% of the voting power at any time during the previous year.
C. Ownership of at least 50% of the equity shares.
D. Holding a managerial position with 5% voting power.
Explanation: Section 64(2) Explanation defines 'substantial interest' as holding (beneficially) shares carrying not less than 10% voting power at any time during the previous year.
Hard NORMAL · Both Spouses Substantial Interest | Section 64(1)(ii) | Higher Income
Both Mr. X and his wife Mrs. X have substantial interest in M/s ABC Enterprises. Mrs. X is employed in the firm without professional qualifications and receives salary. In whose hands will this salary be clubbed?
A. In the hands of Mrs. X herself.
B. In the hands of Mr. X.
C. In the hands of the parent whose total income is higher. ✔
D. Equally in the hands of both Mr. X and Mrs. X.
Explanation: Where both husband and wife have substantial interest in a concern and receive remuneration without technical/professional qualifications, the income is included in the total income of the spouse whose total income (excluding such remuneration) is higher.
Medium NORMAL · HUF Conversion | Section 64(2) | Individual Property
If an individual converts their self-acquired property into property of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) without adequate consideration, how is the income from such property treated?
A. Taxed solely in the hands of the individual.
B. Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
C. Deemed to be income of the individual and clubbed in their total income under section 64(2). ✔
D. Exempt from tax.
Explanation: Under section 64(2), if a member of an HUF converts or transfers their separate property into HUF property without adequate consideration, the income derived from such property is deemed to be the income of the individual member, not the HUF.
Hard NORMAL · HUF Partition | Section 64(2) | Spouse Income
Subsequent to the partition of an HUF where property converted under section 64(2) was distributed, how is the income derived by the spouse of the individual from such distributed property taxed?
A. Taxed in the hands of the spouse.
B. Deemed to be the income of the individual member and clubbed under section 64(2). ✔
C. Exempt from taxation.
D. Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
Explanation: Section 64(2) specifies that where the converted property is partitioned (total or partial), the income derived by the spouse of the individual from the portion received on partition is deemed to arise to the individual and is clubbed in their total income.
Hard NORMAL · Cross-Transfers | Indirect Transfer | Judicial Precedents
Can cross-transfers of assets (e.g., Mr. A gifts to Mrs. B and Mr. B gifts to Mrs. A) be arranged to avoid clubbing provisions under section 64?
A. Yes, clubbing provisions apply only to direct transfers.
B. No, the Supreme Court held that in case of cross-transfers, the transferors will be treated as indirect transferors and income will be clubbed. ✔
C. Yes, provided the gifts are of equal value.
D. No, but only if the gifts are made in different financial years.
Explanation: Under the doctrine of cross-transfers (established by judicial precedents like CIT v. Keshavji Morarji), if transfers are interconnected and form part of a single transaction, the indirect transferor concept applies, and income is clubbed in the respective spouse's hands.
Easy NORMAL · Minor to Major | Section 64(1A) | Cessation of Clubbing
Mr. P gifted Rs. 5,00,000 to his minor daughter. The daughter deposited the amount in a bank earning 8% interest per annum. The interest is clubbed with Mr. P’s income. Next year, the daughter becomes a major. Will the interest earned post-majority be clubbed?
A. Yes, because the initial asset was gifted by the father.
B. No, clubbing of minor's income ceases once the child attains majority. ✔
C. Yes, until the daughter withdraws the principal.
D. No, but only if the daughter files a separate return.
Explanation: Clubbing under section 64(1A) applies strictly during minority. Once the child attains majority, any income earned thereafter is assessed directly in the hands of the child and is not clubbed with the parent's income.
Medium NORMAL · Computation | Clubbing Rules | Net Income
Which of the following is correct regarding the computation of total income when clubbing provisions apply?
A. The income to be clubbed is computed after allowing all deductions and losses pertaining to that income. ✔
B. Gross income is clubbed without deducting any expenses.
C. Only net profit without any deductions is clubbed.
D. Clubbing applies only to capital gains and not to other heads of income.
Explanation: When income is clubbed under sections 60 to 64, it is computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act, meaning all permissible deductions, expenses, and losses relating to that specific income are accounted for before clubbing the net amount.
Hard NORMAL · Deemed Owner | Minor | House Property | Clubbing
Mr. E transfers his house property to his minor son for inadequate consideration. The property is let out. Under whose income tax return will the rental income be computed and clubbed?
A. The minor son
B. The father (Mr. E) as deemed owner under section 27 and clubbing under section 64(1A) ✔
C. The mother
D. Exempt under section 10
Explanation: Mr. E is the deemed owner under section 27(i) due to transfer to a minor child for inadequate consideration. Further, minor's income is clubbed with the parent under section 64(1A). Thus, the rental income (computed under House Property) is included in the father's total income.
Hard NORMAL · Minor Losses | Set-off | Clubbing Provisions
Can a loss under a particular head of income earned by a minor child be clubbed with the income of the parent?
A. No, losses of a minor can never be clubbed.
B. Yes, losses can be clubbed and set off against the parent's income subject to normal set-off rules. ✔
C. Only capital losses can be clubbed, not business losses.
D. Losses are carried forward only by the minor upon attaining majority.
Explanation: Just as income of a minor is clubbed, any loss incurred by the minor (e.g., under capital gains or business) is also clubbed with the parent's income and can be set off against the parent's income as per normal provisions of the Act.
Medium NORMAL · Agreement to Live Apart | Section 64(1)(iv) | Exception
An individual transfers shares to his spouse pursuant to an agreement to live apart (divorce/separation agreement). Is the dividend income from such shares clubbed in the hands of the individual?
A. Yes, because the transfer was to the spouse.
B. No, transfers in connection with an agreement to live apart are specifically excluded from clubbing under section 64(1)(iv). ✔
C. Yes, unless judicial separation is finalized.
D. No, but only if the transfer is for adequate consideration.
Explanation: Section 64(1)(iv) contains an explicit exception: income from assets transferred to a spouse in connection with an agreement to live apart is not clubbed in the transferor's hands.
Medium NORMAL · Sister-in-law | Scope of Clubbing | Section 64
Mr. F gifted Rs. 2,00,000 to his sister-in-law (wife's sister). The sister-in-law invested in shares and earned dividend income. How is this dividend income taxed?
A. Clubbed in the income of Mr. F.
B. Clubbed in the income of Mr. F's wife.
C. Taxed in the hands of the sister-in-law; no clubbing applies. ✔
D. Exempt from tax.
Explanation: Clubbing provisions under section 64 apply only to transfers to spouse, minor child, son's wife, or specified trust beneficiaries. A sister-in-law is not covered under section 64, so the income is taxed in her own hands.
Easy NORMAL · Adequate Consideration | Section 64 | Exclusion
If an asset is transferred for adequate consideration, do the clubbing provisions under section 64 apply?
A. Yes, always.
B. No, clubbing provisions apply strictly to transfers made otherwise than for adequate consideration (except in specific cases like section 60). ✔
C. Yes, if the transfer is between relatives.
D. No, unless approved by the Assessing Officer.
Explanation: Most clauses of section 64 (such as transfers to spouse, daughter-in-law) apply only when the transfer is made 'otherwise than for adequate consideration'. If adequate consideration is paid, clubbing does not apply.
Medium NORMAL · Tax Liability | Clubbed Income | Assessment
Which of the following describes the nature of tax liability when income is clubbed under section 64?
A. The recipient of income pays the tax.
B. The assessee in whose total income the income is clubbed is liable to pay tax on such clubbed income. ✔
C. Tax is paid jointly by the transferor and transferee.
D. The income is taxed at a flat rate of 30%.
Explanation: When income is clubbed, it is included in the total income of the assessee (parent/transferor) and forms part of their total taxable income, making them liable to pay tax thereon according to their applicable slab rates.
Easy NORMAL · Major Child | Gift | Exclusion from Clubbing
Mr. G gifted a commercial building to his major son. The rental income from the building is received by the son. How is this income assessed?
A. Clubbed in the total income of Mr. G.
B. Assessed directly in the hands of the major son. ✔
C. Divided equally between father and son.
D. Taxed in the hands of Mr. G's HUF.
Explanation: Clubbing provisions for gifts to children apply exclusively to minor children under section 64(1A). Gifts to major children are not clubbed; the major son is taxed directly on the rental income.
Medium NORMAL · Capital Gains | Section 64(1)(iv) | Transfer to Spouse
Under section 64(1)(iv), if an asset is transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration, and the spouse subsequently sells the asset at a capital gain, how is the capital gain treated?
A. The capital gain is taxable in the hands of the spouse.
B. The capital gain is clubbed in the total income of the transferor spouse. ✔
C. Exempt from capital gains tax.
D. Shared equally between husband and wife.
Explanation: Capital gains arising from the sale of an asset transferred to a spouse for inadequate consideration are also clubbed in the total income of the transferor spouse under section 64(1)(iv).
Easy NORMAL · Objective | Anti-Tax-Avoidance | Clubbing
What is the primary objective of enacting the clubbing of income provisions (Sections 60 to 64) under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
A. To increase government revenue through double taxation.
B. To prevent tax avoidance and tax evasion through splitting of income among family members. ✔
C. To simplify the filing of tax returns for HUFs.
D. To encourage gifts within families.
Explanation: Clubbing provisions are anti-tax-avoidance measures designed to curb the practice of taxpayers reducing their tax burden by transferring income or assets to family members (spouse, minor children) in lower tax brackets.
Hard NORMAL · Deferred Income | Trust | Minor Child | Section 64(1A)
Mr. H settles an irrevocable trust where the income is accumulated for the benefit of his minor daughter, to be handed over to her when she turns 25. When is this accumulated income taxed?
A. Taxed in the hands of the trust when accumulated.
B. Clubbed in the total income of Mr. H in the year it arises. ✔
C. Taxed when the daughter turns 25.
D. Exempt until distribution.
Explanation: Even if income is accumulated or deferred for the minor child's future benefit under a trust or otherwise, section 64(1A) requires it to be clubbed in the income of the parent in the year the income arises.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rajesh, a resident individual, owns a bungalow and 5,000 shares in X Ltd. On 1st May 2025, he transfers the bungalow to his wife, Mrs. Priya, without adequate consideration. Priya lets out the bungalow for a monthly rent of Rs. 40,000. On 1st June 2025, Rajesh gifts 2,000 shares of X Ltd. to his minor daughter, Riya. Riya receives a dividend of Rs. 20,000 from X Ltd. during the previous year 2025-26. Riya also earns Rs. 15,000 from participating in a national-level dance reality show based on her specialized dancing skills. Rajesh's total income before clubbing is Rs. 12,00,000, while Priya's total income before clubbing is Rs. 5,00,000.
Medium SCENARIO · Deemed Owner | House Property | Section 27
Who is deemed to be the owner of the bungalow transferred by Mr. Rajesh to Mrs. Priya under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
A. Mrs. Priya
B. Mr. Rajesh ✔
C. Both Rajesh and Priya as co-owners
D. The tenant occupying the bungalow
Explanation: As per section 27(i), an individual who transfers a house property to their spouse otherwise than for adequate consideration is deemed to be the owner of the house property.
Medium SCENARIO · House Property Computation | Clubbing | Deemed Owner
How will the rental income from the bungalow be computed and taxed for the previous year 2025-26?
A. Taxed in the hands of Mrs. Priya after standard deduction.
B. Computed in the hands of Mr. Rajesh as deemed owner and clubbed under section 64. ✔
C. Divided equally between Rajesh and Priya.
D. Exempt from tax under section 10.
Explanation: Since Mr. Rajesh is the deemed owner under section 27, the income from house property is computed in his hands and included in his total income.
Medium SCENARIO · Minor Income | Higher Income Parent | Section 10(32)
How will the dividend income of Rs. 20,000 received by minor daughter Riya be treated for tax purposes?
A. Taxed directly in Riya's hands.
B. Clubbed in the total income of Mrs. Priya since Priya's income is lower.
C. Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Rajesh since Rajesh's total income is higher. ✔
D. Exempt up to Rs. 20,000.
Explanation: Minor child's income is clubbed in the income of the parent whose total income is higher. Rajesh's income (Rs. 12L) is higher than Priya's (Rs. 5L), so the dividend is clubbed with Rajesh's income, eligible for section 10(32) exemption.
Hard SCENARIO · Specialized Talent | Minor Exception | Section 64(1A)
How will the income of Rs. 15,000 earned by Riya from the dance reality show be taxed?
A. Clubbed in Mr. Rajesh's total income.
B. Clubbed in Mrs. Priya's total income.
C. Taxed directly in the hands of minor Riya and not clubbed. ✔
D. Exempt from income tax entirely.
Explanation: Income earned by a minor child from an activity involving the application of specialized skills or talent (like dance reality show) is exempt from clubbing under section 64(1A) and is taxed directly in the minor's hands.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Vikram holds a 15% equity stake (substantial interest) in Apex Ltd. His wife, Mrs. Sunita, is appointed as a receptionist in Apex Ltd. with a monthly salary of Rs. 50,000. Sunita does not possess any professional or technical qualifications relevant to the job. Additionally, Vikram gifts Rs. 3,00,000 in cash to his son’s wife, Anita, on 10th August 2025. Anita invests this cash in fixed deposits earning an interest of Rs. 24,000 during the financial year 2025-26. Vikram’s total income before clubbing is Rs. 15,00,000 and Sunita's total income before salary is Rs. 4,00,000.
Medium SCENARIO · Spouse Remuneration | Substantial Interest | Section 64(1)(ii)
How will the salary received by Mrs. Sunita from Apex Ltd. be taxed for the previous year 2025-26?
A. Taxed in the hands of Mrs. Sunita under salaries.
B. Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Vikram under section 64(1)(ii). ✔
C. Disallowed as company expenditure and tax-free for Sunita.
D. Divided equally between Vikram and Sunita.
Explanation: Since Mr. Vikram has a substantial interest in Apex Ltd. (15% voting power) and Sunita receives remuneration without possessing technical or professional qualifications, the salary is clubbed in Vikram's total income under section 64(1)(ii).
Medium SCENARIO · Daughter-in-law | Section 64(1)(vi) | Clubbing
How will the interest income of Rs. 24,000 earned by daughter-in-law Anita be treated under the Income-tax Act?
A. Taxed in the hands of Anita.
B. Clubbed in the total income of Mr. Vikram. ✔
C. Clubbed in the total income of Vikram's son.
D. Exempt under section 10(15).
Explanation: Section 64(1)(vi) mandates that income from assets transferred to a daughter-in-law otherwise than for adequate consideration is clubbed in the total income of the transferor (Mr. Vikram).
Medium SCENARIO · Professional Qualification | Exception | Spouse Salary
What would be the tax treatment of Sunita's salary if she possessed a recognized professional degree and was employed based on her professional qualifications?
A. It would still be clubbed in Mr. Vikram's income.
B. It would be taxable directly in the hands of Mrs. Sunita and NOT clubbed. ✔
C. It would be taxed in the hands of Apex Ltd.
D. It would be exempt from income tax.
Explanation: The clubbing provision under section 64(1)(ii) does not apply if the spouse possesses technical or professional qualifications and the income is solely attributable to the application of such qualifications.
Hard SCENARIO · Accretion of Income | Daughter-in-law | Clubbing Limit
Suppose Anita reinvests the interest of Rs. 24,000 earned from the fixed deposit into mutual funds and earns a further return of Rs. 3,000. What amount is clubbed in Mr. Vikram's hands with respect to Anita?
A. Rs. 27,000
B. Rs. 24,000 ✔
C. Rs. 3,000
D. Nil
Explanation: Only the direct income from the transferred asset (interest of Rs. 24,000) is clubbed. Income from the accretion or reinvestment of such income (Rs. 3,000) is not clubbed.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Kuber, an individual, converts his self-acquired commercial property worth Rs. 50,00,000 into the property of his Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) on 1st July 2025 without receiving any consideration. The HUF lets out this property and earns a rental income of Rs. 3,00,000 during the financial year 2025-26. On 1st January 2026, a total partition of the HUF takes place, and the commercial property is distributed equally among Kuber, his wife, and his major son.
Medium SCENARIO · HUF Conversion | Section 64(2) | Clubbing
How is the rental income of Rs. 3,00,000 earned by the HUF up to the date of partition taxed?
A. Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
B. Deemed to be the income of Mr. Kuber and clubbed in his total income under section 64(2). ✔
C. Divided among all family members equally.
D. Exempt from tax.
Explanation: Under section 64(2), when an individual converts their separate property into HUF property without adequate consideration, the income derived from such property is deemed to be the income of the individual member (Mr. Kuber), not the HUF.
Hard SCENARIO · HUF Partition | Spouse Share | Section 64(2)
Following the total partition on 1st January 2026, how will the rental income attributable to the share received by Mr. Kuber's wife be taxed?
A. Taxed in the hands of the wife.
B. Deemed to be the income of Mr. Kuber and included in his total income. ✔
C. Taxed in the hands of the HUF post-partition.
D. Exempt from tax.
Explanation: Section 64(2) specifically provides that upon partition of an HUF, income derived by the spouse of the individual from the converted property received on partition is deemed to arise to the individual and is clubbed in their total income.
Hard SCENARIO · Major Son | HUF Partition | Tax Assessment
How will the rental income attributable to the share received by the major son upon partition be taxed?
A. Clubbed in Mr. Kuber's total income.
B. Taxed directly in the hands of the major son. ✔
C. Taxed in the hands of the HUF.
D. Exempt from tax.
Explanation: Section 64(2) clubbing on partition applies to the portion received by the spouse of the individual, not to the portion received by children (especially major children). Thus, the major son is taxed directly on his share.
Medium SCENARIO · Legal Fiction | Section 64(2) | HUF Property
What is the legal fiction created under section 64(2) when a member converts separate property into HUF property?
A. The property is treated as sold, attracting capital gains.
B. The property is treated as remaining the individual property of the member for income-tax assessment of its yield. ✔
C. The HUF is treated as a corporate entity.
D. The income is treated as agricultural income.
Explanation: Section 64(2) creates a statutory fiction whereby income from property converted by a member to HUF property without adequate consideration is treated as income of the individual member rather than the HUF.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. and Mrs. Sharma have a minor son, Master Kunal, aged 10 years. Mr. Sharma's total income before any clubbing is Rs. 18,00,000, and Mrs. Sharma's total income before any clubbing is Rs. 22,00,000. Mr. Sharma gifts Rs. 10,00,000 to Kunal out of his personal savings. Kunal deposits this money in a corporate fixed deposit on 1st April 2025 at an interest rate of 10% per annum, earning Rs. 1,00,000 as interest during the financial year 2025-26. Additionally, Kunal wins a prize of Rs. 50,000 in a state-level chess championship.
Medium SCENARIO · Minor Income | Higher Income Parent | Section 64(1A)
In whose total income shall the interest income of Rs. 1,00,000 earned by minor Kunal be included?
A. Mr. Sharma, being the donor of the asset.
B. Mrs. Sharma, because her total income is higher than Mr. Sharma's. ✔
C. Master Kunal, in his individual return.
D. Divided equally between Mr. and Mrs. Sharma.
Explanation: Section 64(1A) mandates that the income of a minor child is included in the total income of the parent whose total income (excluding the minor's income) is higher. Since Mrs. Sharma's income (Rs. 22L) exceeds Mr. Sharma's (Rs. 18L), it is clubbed with Mrs. Sharma.
Easy SCENARIO · Section 10(32) | Minor Exemption | Limit
What amount of exemption under section 10(32) is available against the clubbed interest income of Rs. 1,00,000?
A. Rs. 1,00,000
B. Rs. 5,000
C. Rs. 1,500 ✔
D. Nil
Explanation: Section 10(32) grants an exemption of up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child whose income is clubbed under section 64(1A), or the actual income clubbed, whichever is less.
Hard SCENARIO · Talent Exception | Minor Child | Chess Prize
How will the prize of Rs. 50,000 won by Kunal in the chess championship be taxed?
A. Clubbed in Mrs. Sharma's total income.
B. Clubbed in Mr. Sharma's total income.
C. Assessed directly in the hands of minor Kunal and not clubbed. ✔
D. Exempt from tax under section 10.
Explanation: Income earned by a minor child from any activity involving application of specialized skill, talent, or specialized knowledge (such as competitive chess) is excluded from clubbing under section 64(1A) and taxed in the minor's hands.
Medium SCENARIO · Disability Exception | Section 80U | Minor Income
If Master Kunal had a physical disability of the nature specified under section 80U, how would his total income be treated?
A. Clubbed with the higher-earning parent after 80U deduction.
B. Assessed entirely in the hands of Master Kunal without clubbing. ✔
C. Split between the parents equally.
D. Exempt from all income taxes.
Explanation: The proviso to section 64(1A) explicitly states that the income of a minor child suffering from any disability specified under section 80U shall not be clubbed in the parent's income and is taxed directly in the hands of the minor.
CASE SCENARIO: Mr. Rohan and Mr. Sohan are brothers-in-law. On 1st June 2025, Mr. Rohan gifts Rs. 5,00,000 to Mr. Sohan’s wife, Mrs. Meena. Simultaneously, on the same date, Mr. Sohan gifts Rs. 5,00,000 to Mr. Rohan’s wife, Mrs. Shweta. Mrs. Meena invests the gifted amount in debentures earning interest of Rs. 60,000 during the previous year 2025-26. Mrs. Shweta also invests her gifted amount in shares earning dividend income of Rs. 60,000 during the same period.
Medium SCENARIO · Cross-Transfers | Indirect Transfer | Tax Avoidance
What legal principle governs the taxability of income earned by Mrs. Meena and Mrs. Shweta in this scenario?
A. The doctrine of independent gifts.
B. The doctrine of cross-transfers (indirect transfers). ✔
C. The principle of mutual benefit trusts.
D. The rule of corporate tax avoidance.
Explanation: This is a classic case of cross-transfers where interconnected gifts are made to each other's spouses to bypass direct clubbing provisions. The courts treat the transferors as indirect transferors.
Hard SCENARIO · Cross-Transfer Clubbing | Mr. Rohan | Section 64(1)(iv)
In whose total income will the interest income of Rs. 60,000 earned by Mrs. Meena be clubbed?
A. Mr. Sohan, her husband.
B. Mr. Rohan, the actual indirect transferor. ✔
C. Mrs. Meena herself.
D. Equally between Rohan and Sohan.
Explanation: Due to the cross-transfer arrangement, Mr. Rohan is considered the indirect transferor of the assets held by Mrs. Meena. Hence, the income is clubbed in Mr. Rohan's total income under section 64(1)(iv).
Hard SCENARIO · Cross-Transfer Clubbing | Mr. Sohan | Section 64(1)(iv)
In whose total income will the dividend income of Rs. 60,000 earned by Mrs. Shweta be clubbed?
A. Mr. Rohan, her husband.
B. Mr. Sohan, the indirect transferor. ✔
C. Mrs. Shweta herself.
D. Exempt from tax.
Explanation: Applying the cross-transfer rule, Mr. Sohan is treated as the indirect transferor of the assets held by Mrs. Shweta, and consequently, the dividend income is clubbed in Mr. Sohan's total income.
Hard SCENARIO · Independent Transfers | Cross-Transfer Limits | Case Law
Would the clubbing apply if the gifts made by Rohan and Sohan were made in different financial years with no connection or prior agreement between them?
A. Yes, cross-transfer applies regardless of timing.
B. No, if the transfers are independent, genuine, and not part of an interconnected arrangement or quid pro quo, cross-transfers do not apply. ✔
C. Yes, because both are related parties.
D. No, gifts between brothers-in-law are always exempt.
Explanation: Judicial rulings establish that cross-transfers apply only when the transfers are inter-dependent and form part of a synchronized arrangement. If they are independent and lack a quid pro quo, direct clubbing rules apply only to direct spouse transfers.

Paper 3: Taxation · Module 2 · Chapter 5:

Taxation — 55 rows
Easy NORMAL · Set-off of losses | Specified business | Section 35AD
Which of the following losses cannot be set off against any other head of income in the same assessment year under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
A. Business loss of a specified business referred to in section 35AD ✔
B. Loss from house property
C. Loss from a speculative business
D. Loss from an ordinary non-speculative business
Explanation: As per section 73A, any loss computed in respect of any specified business referred to in section 35AD can be set off only against profits and gains, if any, of any other specified business. It cannot be set off against income under any other head.
Medium NORMAL · Inter-source adjustment | Speculative business | Section 73
Under section 70, inter-source adjustment is generally permissible. Which of the following inter-source adjustments is NOT allowed?
A. Loss from house property A set off against income from house property B
B. Loss from a speculative business set off against profit from an ordinary business ✔
C. Loss from an ordinary business set off against income from a speculative business
D. Loss from a non-speculative business set off against income from house property
Explanation: Under section 73(1), any loss computed in respect of a speculative business carried on by the assessee cannot be set off except against profits and gains of another speculative business. Thus, it cannot be set off against ordinary business profits.
Easy NORMAL · Carry forward | Business loss | Section 72
What is the maximum period for which business loss (other than speculation loss and specified business loss) can be carried forward and set off under section 72?
A. 4 assessment years
B. 8 assessment years ✔
C. Indefinitely
D. 10 assessment years
Explanation: Under section 72(3), business loss can be carried forward for a maximum of 8 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed.
Medium NORMAL · Race horses | Section 74A | Other sources
Can a loss from an activity of owning and maintaining race horses be set off against income from salary in the same assessment year?
A. Yes, without any restriction
B. No, it cannot be set off against income under any other head, nor can it be set off against any other source under the head Income from Other Sources ✔
C. Yes, subject to a limit of Rs. 2,00,000
D. Yes, if the assessee maintains regular books of accounts
Explanation: Under section 74A(3), the loss incurred in the activity of owning and maintaining race horses can be set off only against income from the same activity i.e., owning and maintaining race horses. It cannot be set off against any other head or source.
Hard NORMAL · Unabsorbed depreciation | Section 32 | Companies
In the case of a company (other than a company in which public are substantially interested), unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward:
A. For 8 assessment years only
B. For 4 assessment years only
C. Indefinitely, even if there is a change in shareholding ✔
D. Indefinitely, subject to the provisions of section 79
Explanation: As per section 32(2), unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward indefinitely and has no time limit. Unlike business losses, unabsorbed depreciation is not subject to the change in shareholding restrictions under section 79.
Medium NORMAL · Section 79 | Change in shareholding | Business loss
For carrying forward and setting off of accumulated business losses in case of closely held companies, what percentage of voting power must remain continuously beneficially held under section 79?
A. Not less than 51% ✔
B. Not less than 49%
C. Not less than 75%
D. Not less than 26%
Explanation: Section 79 provides that in case of a company in which public are not substantially interested, loss incurred in any year prior to the previous year can be carried forward only if not less than 51% of the voting power is beneficially held by the same persons on the last day of the previous year.
Hard NORMAL · Section 80 | Due date of return | House property loss
Which of the following losses can be carried forward even if the return of income is filed after the due date specified under section 139(1)?
A. Business loss
B. Speculation loss
C. Loss from house property ✔
D. Capital loss
Explanation: As per section 80 read with section 139(3), filing the return of income within the due date under section 139(1) is mandatory for carrying forward business loss, speculation loss, specified business loss, and capital loss. However, loss under the head 'Income from house property' and unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward even if the return is filed late.
Easy NORMAL · Capital losses | Section 74 | Carry forward
What is the maximum period for carrying forward capital losses (both short-term and long-term) under section 74?
A. 4 assessment years
B. 8 assessment years ✔
C. Indefinitely
D. 12 assessment years
Explanation: Under section 74(1) and 74(2), both short-term capital losses and long-term capital losses can be carried forward for a maximum of 8 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year in which the loss was first computed.
Medium NORMAL · Capital gains | Inter-source adjustment | Section 70
Can a long-term capital loss be set off against short-term capital gains in the same assessment year?
A. No, long-term capital loss can only be set off against long-term capital gains
B. Yes, long-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains ✔
C. No, capital losses cannot be set off against capital gains at all
D. Yes, but only up to Rs. 1,00,000
Explanation: Under section 70(3), a long-term capital loss can be set off against any capital gain, whether short-term or long-term. However, a short-term capital loss can be set off against both short-term and long-term capital gains as well.
Hard NORMAL · Order of set-off | Unabsorbed depreciation | Business loss
What is the order of priority for setting off unabsorbed depreciation, current year business loss, and brought forward business loss?
A. Current year business loss -> Brought forward business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation ✔
B. Current year business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation -> Brought forward business loss
C. Unabsorbed depreciation -> Current year business loss -> Brought forward business loss
D. Brought forward business loss -> Current year business loss -> Unabsorbed depreciation
Explanation: The order of set-off under the Act is: (1) Current year deductions like depreciation, capital expenditure on scientific research, etc.; (2) Current year business loss; (3) Brought forward business loss under section 72; (4) Unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2).
Easy NORMAL · House property loss | Section 71 | Inter-head adjustment
Under section 71(3A), loss from house property can be set off against any other head of income in any assessment year up to a maximum of:
A. Rs. 50,000
B. Rs. 1,00,000
C. Rs. 2,00,000 ✔
D. No limit
Explanation: As per section 71(3A), where the net result of computation under the head 'Income from house property' is a loss, the assessee can set off such loss against income under any other head to the extent of Rs. 2,00,000 in any assessment year.
Medium NORMAL · Salary head | Inter-head adjustment | Section 71
Can a loss under the head 'Income from Salaries' be set off against income under any other head of income?
A. Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
B. Yes, without any limit
C. No, loss under the head 'Salaries' cannot be set off against income under any other head ✔
D. Yes, only against income from house property
Explanation: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, there cannot be a negative income from salary under normal circumstances, but even if a computational loss arises under the head 'Salaries' (e.g., allowances exceeding income), it cannot be set off against income under any other head under section 71.
Easy NORMAL · Speculation loss | Section 73 | Carry forward
For how many assessment years can a speculation loss be carried forward under section 73?
A. 4 assessment years ✔
B. 8 assessment years
C. Indefinitely
D. 6 assessment years
Explanation: Under section 73(4), speculation loss can be carried forward for a maximum of 4 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed.
Easy NORMAL · Section 72 | Business loss | Set-off
Which of the following incomes can be reduced by setting off brought forward business loss under section 72?
A. Income from salary
B. Profits and gains of business or profession ✔
C. Capital gains
D. Winning from lotteries
Explanation: Brought forward business loss under section 72 can be set off only against profits and gains of business or profession.
Medium NORMAL · Partnership firm | Business loss | Assessment entity
Can a registered firm (partnership firm) carry forward and set off its business losses?
A. No, partnership firms cannot carry forward losses
B. Yes, the firm itself carries forward and sets off the loss against its own future business income ✔
C. No, the loss must be allocated to partners for carry forward
D. Yes, but only unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward by the firm
Explanation: A partnership firm (whether registered or not) is a separate assessable entity. Business losses are carried forward by the firm itself to be set off against its future business profits, and not by the partners (except in case of dissolution/discontinuation where specific rules apply).
Hard NORMAL · Unabsorbed depreciation | Section 32 | Priority of set-off
What happens to the unabsorbed depreciation when there is no business income in the current year, but the assessee has income from capital gains and other sources?
A. It lapses permanently
B. It can be set off against capital gains and other sources
C. It can be set off against salary income only
D. It can be carried forward indefinitely, but first must be set off against any other head of income in the current year ✔
Explanation: Under section 32(2), if unabsorbed depreciation cannot be fully set off against business income in the current year, it is added to the depreciation of the next year. However, in the current year, it can be set off against any other head of income (except salary) after inter-head adjustments are exhausted.
Medium NORMAL · Exempt income | Losses | General principles
Can a loss from an exempt source of income be set off against taxable income?
A. Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
B. No, since the income itself is exempt, any related loss cannot be set off against taxable income ✔
C. Yes, under section 71
D. Yes, provided books of accounts are audited
Explanation: Since the income from an exempt source does not form part of total income, any loss incurred from such exempt source cannot be set off against taxable income.
Hard NORMAL · Death of assessee | Legal representative | Business loss
In the event of the death of an assessee, can the legal representative carry forward and set off the business losses of the deceased assessee?
A. Yes, the legal representative can carry forward and set off the deceased's business losses
B. No, business losses lapse upon the death of the assessee ✔
C. Yes, but only for a maximum of 1 year
D. No, only unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward by the legal representative
Explanation: Under the Income-tax Act, business losses of the deceased assessee cannot be carried forward and set off by the legal representative, because the legal representative is not the same assessee who incurred the loss. (Note: This is an exception compared to inheritance of businesses where succession rules apply differently, but personal business loss under Sec 72 lapses upon death).
Easy NORMAL · Section 71B | House property loss | Carry forward
Which section of the Income-tax Act, 1961 deals with the carry forward and set-off of losses from house property?
A. Section 71
B. Section 71B ✔
C. Section 72
D. Section 74
Explanation: Section 71B specifically deals with the carry forward and set-off of loss from house property for up to 8 assessment years against income from house property.
Easy NORMAL · Inter-head adjustment | Business loss | Salary
Can a loss from an ordinary business be set off against salary income in the same assessment year?
A. Yes, without any restrictions
B. Yes, up to Rs. 2,00,000
C. No, business loss cannot be set off against salary income under section 71 ✔
D. Yes, if the business is a proprietary concern
Explanation: Under section 71(2), business loss cannot be set off against income under the head 'Salaries'.
Medium NORMAL · Section 80 | Capital loss | Belated return
Can a short-term capital loss be carried forward if the return of income is filed after the due date under section 139(1)?
A. Yes, always
B. No, section 80 bars the carry forward if the return is filed belatedly ✔
C. Yes, up to 4 years
D. Yes, with the permission of the Principal Commissioner
Explanation: Section 80 mandates that returns for losses under section 72(1) (business loss), section 73(2) (speculation loss), section 73A(2) (specified business loss), section 74(1) (capital loss), and section 74A(3) (race horse loss) must be filed within the due date specified under section 139(1) in order to carry them forward.
Hard NORMAL · Other sources | Set-off | General loss
What is the treatment of losses under the head 'Income from Other Sources' (other than race horses and lotteries)?
A. They cannot be set off against any income
B. They can be set off against any other income under the same head or any other head under inter-source and inter-head rules ✔
C. They can only be carried forward for 8 years
D. They lapse immediately and cannot be set off even within the same head
Explanation: Losses under the head 'Income from Other Sources' (general sources, e.g., loss on maintenance of machinery let out) can be set off against any other income under the same head (inter-source) and against any other head of income (inter-head) under sections 70 and 71, and cannot be carried forward.
Medium NORMAL · Race horses | Section 74A | Carry forward
Can a loss from an activity of owning and maintaining race horses be carried forward?
A. No, it lapses in the same year
B. Yes, for a maximum of 4 assessment years ✔
C. Yes, for a maximum of 8 assessment years
D. Yes, indefinitely
Explanation: Under section 74A(3), loss from the activity of owning and maintaining race horses can be carried forward for a maximum of 4 assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed.
Medium NORMAL · Lottery winnings | Section 58 | Restrictions on set-off
