Medium SCENARIO · Internal Weakness | Financial Controls | Clinical Trials
Zenith Pharma's weak financial controls leading to cost overruns in clinical trials represent a strategic:
A. Core competence
B. Distinctive advantage
C. Internal weakness ✔
D. External opportunity
Explanation: Cost overruns and weak financial controls undermine operational efficiency, classifying them as internal weaknesses that require corrective management intervention.
Medium SCENARIO · Resource-Based View | Core Competencies | Sustainable Advantage
Under the Resource-Based View, how does Zenith Pharma's research team contribute to its competitive position?
A. They provide a baseline threshold capability required by all pharmacies
B. They constitute a valuable, rare, and inimitable resource driving sustainable competitive advantage ✔
C. They serve as a support activity with zero strategic impact
D. They act as an external macroeconomic factor
Explanation: An exceptional R&D team possessing rare and inimitable knowledge serves as a core resource driving sustainable competitive advantage under the RBV framework.
CASE SCENARIO: Apex Retail Corp operates a massive chain of supermarkets across India. Apex uses a state-of-the-art enterprise resource planning (ERP) system that tracks inventory across all stores in real-time, automatically reordering stock from suppliers when inventory dips below specific thresholds. While competitors possess similar ERP software licenses, none have integrated the software with employee incentive structures and daily store routines as effectively as Apex. However, Apex's human resource department suffers from high turnover among store-level floor staff.
Medium SCENARIO · VRIO Framework | Organization | System Integration
The integration of Apex Retail's ERP software with employee incentive structures and store routines best illustrates which concept?
A. Causal transparency
B. Organizational alignment and the 'Organization' pillar of VRIO ✔
C. External threat mitigation
D. Outbound logistics outsourcing
Explanation: Apex successfully coordinates its technological resources with management systems and employee incentives, fulfilling the 'Organization' requirement of the VRIO framework to capture value.
Hard SCENARIO · Causal Ambiguity | Competitive Advantage | Technology Utilization
Even though competitors possess similar ERP software licenses, Apex maintains an advantage because of:
A. Causal ambiguity and complex organizational routines ✔
B. Government subsidies for supermarket software
C. Exclusivity agreements with software developers
D. Zero employee turnover
Explanation: When rivals have access to the same technology (software licenses) but cannot match performance because the specific integration methods are unclear or complex, causal ambiguity protects the firm's advantage.
Medium SCENARIO · Value Chain Analysis | Inbound Logistics | Procurement
In Porter's Value Chain, the automated reordering of stock from suppliers when inventory dips falls primarily under which activity?
A. Inbound Logistics and Procurement ✔
B. Firm Infrastructure
C. Marketing and Sales
D. After-sales Service
Explanation: Managing incoming inventory, warehousing, and purchasing inputs from suppliers constitutes inbound logistics and procurement support activities.
Medium SCENARIO · Internal Weakness | Human Resources | Operational Risk
How does the high turnover among store-level floor staff impact Apex Retail's strategic posture?
A. It strengthens customer service consistency
B. It represents an internal weakness that could threaten service quality and operational execution ✔
C. It has no relevance to internal environment analysis
D. It automatically guarantees higher profit margins
Explanation: High frontline staff turnover is an internal weakness that can disrupt store-level execution, diminish customer experience, and strain HR management.
CASE SCENARIO: Delta Financial Services (DFS) provides corporate lending and advisory services. DFS management recently conducted a benchmarking exercise against top global investment banks. The study revealed that while DFS processes loan applications faster than any domestic competitor, its risk-assessment analytics for cross-border transactions lag significantly behind global benchmarks. Furthermore, DFS has a rigid corporate culture that discourages junior analysts from reporting anomalous risk data upward.
Medium SCENARIO · Benchmarking | Best Practices | Performance Analysis
The comparison conducted by Delta Financial Services against top global investment banks is an example of:
A. Internal historical budgeting
B. Benchmarking ✔
C. Macroeconomic forecasting
D. Value chain outsourcing
Explanation: Comparing organizational processes and performance metrics against industry leaders or best-in-class peers is known as benchmarking.
Medium SCENARIO · Distinctive Competence | Internal Strength | Operational Speed
DFS's ability to process loan applications faster than domestic competitors represents a:
A. Threshold capability
B. Distinctive competence / Strength ✔
C. Critical regulatory weakness
D. Macroeconomic threat
Explanation: Performing an activity faster and better than domestic competitors establishes a clear internal strength and potential distinctive competence.
Hard SCENARIO · Organizational Culture | Internal Weakness | Risk Management
The rigid corporate culture discouraging junior analysts from reporting risk data upward creates which internal strategic vulnerability?
A. A structural barrier to effective internal communication and risk mitigation (Weakness) ✔
B. An impenetrable VRIO-compliant inimitable resource
C. An optimal financial capital structure
D. A flawless firm infrastructure
Explanation: A culture that suppresses critical risk communication creates dangerous blind spots, representing a severe internal weakness in firm infrastructure and management control.
Medium SCENARIO · Benchmarking | Competitive Benchmarking | Industry Leaders
What type of benchmarking did DFS perform when comparing its operational speed and risk analytics against top global investment banks?
A. Internal benchmarking across regional branch offices
B. Competitive / Functional benchmarking against industry leaders ✔
C. Statutory benchmarking mandated by RBI
D. Historical benchmarking against DFS's own 2010 performance
Explanation: Comparing performance metrics against external leading peers (global investment banks) constitutes competitive or functional benchmarking.
CASE SCENARIO: Omega Tech Solutions specializes in enterprise cloud migration. Omega's primary value driver is its proprietary software migration toolkit, which reduces client downtime by 70%. The toolkit is legally protected by international patents. However, Omega's sales and marketing team is weak, relying entirely on word-of-mouth referrals rather than proactive outreach. As a result, aggressive competitors with inferior software are capturing larger market shares through aggressive advertising.
Medium SCENARIO · Resource-Based View | Intangible Resources | Patents
Omega Tech Solutions' proprietary software migration toolkit protected by international patents is best classified under the Resource-Based View as:
A. A tangible financial asset
B. A valuable, rare, and legally protected intangible resource ✔
C. A threshold capability available to all firms
D. An outbound logistics support function
Explanation: Patents and proprietary software tools are valuable, rare, intangible intellectual property assets that form the foundation of a firm's competitive advantage.
Medium SCENARIO · Value Chain Analysis | Marketing and Sales | Primary Activities
In Porter's Value Chain, Omega's reliance on word-of-mouth referrals due to a weak sales and marketing team indicates a deficiency in which primary activity?
A. Marketing and Sales ✔
B. Inbound Logistics
C. Technology Development
D. Firm Infrastructure
Explanation: Marketing and Sales is a primary value chain activity responsible for customer acquisition, advertising, pricing, and channel management.
Hard SCENARIO · Strategic Balance | Marketing Weakness | Competitor Dynamics
Why are competitors with inferior software able to capture larger market shares than Omega Tech Solutions?
A. Because Omega's superior product is offset by its internal weakness in marketing and sales execution
B. Because inferior software always outperforms superior technology in the long run ✔
C. Because patents are illegal in the tech industry
D. Because Omega has zero operating margins
Explanation: Wait, let's check option index. Option 0 is 'Because Omega's superior product is offset by its internal weakness in marketing and sales execution'. Let's check index: index 0 is correct.
Medium SCENARIO · Strategic Realignment | Functional Capabilities | Marketing Investment
How should Omega Tech Solutions strategically realign its internal activities to capitalize on its proprietary software toolkit?
A. Divest the software toolkit and focus solely on accounting
B. Invest in strengthening its marketing and sales capabilities to actively promote its superior migration toolkit ✔
C. Outsource R&D to competitors
D. Reduce patent protection voluntarily
Explanation: To overcome market share losses, Omega must address its functional weakness by upgrading its marketing and sales execution to match the excellence of its technology.

Paper 6: Financial Management and Strategic Management · Paper 6B · Chapter 4:

SM — 55 rows
Easy NORMAL · Porter Generic Strategies | Differentiation | Strategic Choices
Which of the following strategic alternatives represents a strategy followed by an enterprise when it aims at high market share, high quality, and premium pricing?
A. Cost Leadership
B. Differentiation ✔
C. Focus
D. Retrenchment
Explanation: Differentiation strategy involves creating products or services that are perceived industry-wide as unique, allowing the firm to charge premium prices. It focuses on quality, brand loyalty, and distinct features rather than lowest cost. This is a core component of Michael Porter's Generic Strategies.
Easy NORMAL · Ansoff Matrix | Product Development | Strategic Alternatives
Ansoff's Product-Market Growth Matrix suggests four strategic alternatives. Which strategy involves introducing new products into existing markets?
A. Market Penetration
B. Product Development ✔
C. Market Development
D. Diversification
Explanation: Product Development involves developing new products and aiming them at existing markets. Ansoff's Matrix uses existing vs. new grids for products and markets to chart growth directions. It helps organizations assess risks associated with different growth paths.
Easy NORMAL · Retrenchment | Divestment | Strategic Choices
When a firm decides to sell off a division or part of its business unit to a strategic buyer or spin it off as an independent company, it is executing which type of retrenchment strategy?
A. Turnaround Strategy
B. Divestment Strategy ✔
C. Liquidation Strategy
D. Combination Strategy
Explanation: Divestment strategy involves selling or liquidating a portion of a business, or a major division, usually as part of a rehabilitation plan or to exit unprofitable segments. Turnaround focuses on operational recovery, while liquidation involves closing down the entire enterprise.
Easy NORMAL · BCG Matrix | Portfolio Analysis | Strategic Choices
Which strategic choice matrix evaluates business portfolios based on industry growth rate and relative market share?
A. Ansoff Matrix
B. BCG Growth-Share Matrix ✔
C. ADL Matrix
D. GE Nine-Cell Matrix
Explanation: The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) Growth-Share Matrix classifies a firm's SBU portfolio using two dimensions: relative market share (horizontal axis) and industry growth rate (vertical axis). It categorizes them into Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks, and Dogs.
Easy NORMAL · BCG Matrix | Cash Cows | Portfolio Management
In the BCG Growth-Share Matrix, SBUs that generate high cash flows but operate in low-growth industries are classified as:
A. Stars
B. Question Marks
C. Cash Cows ✔
D. Dogs
Explanation: Cash Cows are low-growth, high-share businesses that generate heavy cash flows. Because growth is low, investments required are minimal, making them sources of cash for other units. Stars have high growth and high share, requiring high investment.
Easy NORMAL · Porter Generic Strategies | Focus Strategy | Strategic Choices
Which of Porter's Generic Strategies involves targeting a narrow buyer segment or niche and tailoring the product strategy to the specific tastes and requirements of that niche?
A. Cost Leadership Strategy
B. Broad Differentiation Strategy
C. Focus Strategy ✔
D. Integration Strategy
Explanation: Focus strategy concentrates on a narrow segment (buyer group, product line, or geographic market) and aims to achieve either cost advantage or differentiation within that specific niche. It can be cost-focus or differentiation-focus.
Easy NORMAL · Ansoff Matrix | Growth Strategies | Strategic Choices
Which of the following is NOT one of the strategies identified under Ansoff's Product-Market Growth Matrix?
A. Market Penetration
B. Market Development
C. Cost Rationalization ✔
D. Diversification
Explanation: Cost Rationalization is not part of Ansoff's Matrix. The four strategies in Ansoff's matrix are Market Penetration, Market Development, Product Development, and Diversification, focusing entirely on growth directions.
Easy NORMAL · Cost Leadership | Porter Generic Strategies | Competitive Advantage
A strategy where a firm seeks to achieve lowest overall costs on industry-wide basis through large-scale operations and tight cost controls is called:
A. Cost Leadership ✔
B. Differentiation
C. Focus
D. Alliance
Explanation: Cost Leadership is a generic strategy aimed at establishing a competitive advantage by having the lowest cost of operation in the industry. It relies on economies of scale, learning curve effects, and stringent cost minimization.
Easy NORMAL · Diversification | Conglomerate | Strategic Choices
When a firm enters into a completely new business that has no relation to its existing technology, products, or markets, it is practicing:
A. Concentric Diversification
B. Horizontal Diversification
C. Conglomerate Diversification ✔
D. Vertical Integration
Explanation: Conglomerate diversification involves moving into entirely new areas that are unrelated to the current business in terms of customer base, technology, or products. Concentric and horizontal diversifications involve varying degrees of relatedness.
Easy NORMAL · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | Portfolio Analysis | Strategic Choices
Which portfolio analysis matrix utilizes industry attractiveness and business strength as its two composite dimensions?
A. BCG Matrix
B. Ansoff Matrix
C. GE Nine-Cell Matrix ✔
D. ADL Matrix
Explanation: The General Electric (GE) Nine-Cell Matrix evaluates business portfolios using 'Industry Attractiveness' and 'Business Strength' as its two composite dimensions, offering a more nuanced multi-factor analysis than the BCG matrix.
Medium NORMAL · Ansoff Matrix | Market Development | Strategic Choices
An established electronics company enters the overseas market by selling its existing product line to new geographic segments. According to Ansoff's Matrix, this is:
A. Market Penetration
B. Market Development ✔
C. Product Development
D. Diversification
Explanation: Market Development involves taking existing products into new markets, such as geographical expansion or targeting new customer segments. This expands the firm's customer base without altering the core product offering significantly.
Medium NORMAL · Vertical Integration | Backward Integration | Corporate Strategy
Which of the following correctly describes 'Backward Integration' in the context of vertical integration strategies?
A. Acquiring or merging with competitors in the same industry.
B. Grasping control over suppliers of raw materials or components. ✔
C. Setting up distribution channels closer to the final consumer.
D. Diversifying into completely unrelated industries.
Explanation: Backward integration involves moving upstream in the supply chain by taking over the supply sources or manufacturing of raw materials. Forward integration involves moving downstream toward the end consumer.
Medium NORMAL · Turnaround Strategy | Retrenchment | Strategic Choices
Turnaround strategy is typically deployed when an organization experiences persistent losses and declining performance. Which step is generally initiated first in a turnaround situation?
A. Aggressive market expansion
B. Massive capital expenditure in new plants
C. Cost cutting and asset reduction ✔
D. Diversification into new segments
Explanation: The initial stage of a turnaround strategy involves retrenchment measures, such as cost cutting, shedding unprofitable assets, freezing hiring, and stopping cash bleed to stabilize the firm before embarking on recovery and growth.
Medium NORMAL · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | Hold Strategy | Portfolio Matrix
In the context of the GE Nine-Cell Matrix, if an SBU falls into a cell representing medium industry attractiveness and medium business strength, what is the standard strategic prescription?
A. Invest/Grow aggressively
B. Harvest/Divest
C. Hold/Selectivity/Earnings preservation ✔
D. Liquidate immediately
Explanation: Cells in the middle of the GE matrix typically warrant a 'Hold' or 'Wait and See' strategy, focusing on selectivity and maintaining earnings rather than pouring massive new capital or liquidating.
Medium NORMAL · Backward Integration | Integration Strategies | Strategic Choices
A company manufacturing biscuits decides to acquire a packaging material manufacturing unit that previously supplied boxes to them. This is an example of:
A. Forward Integration
B. Backward Integration ✔
C. Horizontal Integration
D. Conglomerate Diversification
Explanation: Acquiring a supplier of inputs (packaging material) is backward integration as it moves the firm backward along the industry value chain toward raw material/component production.
Medium NORMAL · Porter Generic Strategies | Stuck in the Middle | Competitive Strategy
Why might a firm choose a 'Stuck in the Middle' position according to Michael Porter, and what is its consequence?
A. It deliberately combines low cost and high differentiation for superior profitability.
B. It fails to commit to either cost leadership or differentiation, resulting in below-average performance. ✔
C. It dominates both niche and broad markets simultaneously.
D. It achieves monopoly status through price fixing.
Explanation: Porter warns that being 'stuck in the middle'—failing to establish a clear cost or differentiation advantage—is a recipe for strategic failure, as the firm lacks the low cost to compete with cost leaders or the uniqueness to command premium prices.
Medium NORMAL · ADL Matrix | Industry Life Cycle | Strategic Choices
Which matrix classifies industries based on their stage of development (embryonic, growth, mature, aging) and the firm's competitive position (dominant, strong, favorable, tenable, weak)?
A. BCG Matrix
B. ADL Matrix ✔
C. Ansoff Matrix
D. GE Nine-Cell Matrix
Explanation: The Arthur D. Little (ADL) Matrix uses the industry life cycle stage and the firm's competitive position as its two axes, leading to 24 distinct cells to guide strategic choice.
Medium NORMAL · Liquidation Strategy | Retrenchment | Strategic Choices
Under what condition is a 'Liquidation Strategy' considered the most appropriate choice for a firm?
A. When the firm wants to expand into international markets.
B. When all turnaround and divestment efforts have failed and continuing operations will only accumulate more losses. ✔
C. When the firm is a Cash Cow generating excessive surplus funds.
D. When the firm wants to achieve cost leadership through economies of scale.
Explanation: Liquidation is the most extreme and final retrenchment strategy, chosen when all other restructuring, turnaround, or divestment options have proven unsuccessful and bankruptcy or closure is inevitable.
Medium NORMAL · Diversification | Concentric | Conglomerate
What distinguishes 'Concentric Diversification' from 'Conglomerate Diversification'?
A. Concentric involves related technology or markets, whereas conglomerate involves completely unrelated businesses. ✔
B. Concentric involves selling assets, whereas conglomerate involves asset acquisition.
C. Concentric is a retrenchment strategy, whereas conglomerate is an expansion strategy.
D. Concentric is done only domestically, while conglomerate is international.
Explanation: Concentric diversification happens when a company expands into businesses that are related to its existing operations through technology, marketing, or products. Conglomerate diversification involves entering completely unrelated fields.
Medium NORMAL · Ansoff Matrix | Market Penetration | Strategic Choices
A firm adopts a strategy to increase market share for its present products in existing markets through greater marketing efforts and aggressive pricing. This is known as:
A. Market Development
B. Market Penetration ✔
C. Product Development
D. Horizontal Integration
Explanation: Market Penetration is focused on increasing sales of existing products in existing markets through intensive marketing, promotional campaigns, and pricing adjustments, without changing product or market definitions.
Medium NORMAL · Cost Leadership | Risks | Porter Generic Strategies
In the context of Porter's Generic Strategies, a firm pursuing a Cost Leadership strategy must guard against which of the following primary risks?
A. Loss of customer loyalty due to extreme focus on uniqueness
B. Technological breakthroughs by rivals that render cost-saving methods obsolete ✔
C. Inability to achieve high enough margins to cover high R&D costs
D. Fragmented customer base requiring tailored products
Explanation: A major risk of cost leadership is that technological innovations or changes in manufacturing processes by competitors can overnight neutralize the cost advantage built on older capital investments or scale.
Medium NORMAL · Horizontal Integration | Expansion Strategy | Strategic Choices
When two companies operating in the same industry at the same stage of the value chain decide to combine their operations, the strategy is called:
A. Vertical Integration
B. Horizontal Integration ✔
C. Backward Integration
D. Conglomerate Diversification
Explanation: Horizontal integration involves a firm acquiring or merging with competitors operating at the same stage of the industry value chain, typically to increase market share, achieve economies of scale, or reduce competition.
Hard NORMAL · BCG Matrix | Criticisms | Portfolio Management
Which portfolio framework categorizes business units as 'Stars', 'Cash Cows', 'Question Marks', and 'Dogs', but has been criticized for oversimplifying complex market dynamics into a two-dimensional grid?
A. GE Nine-Cell Matrix
B. BCG Growth-Share Matrix ✔
C. ADL Matrix
D. Ansoff Matrix
Explanation: The BCG Growth-Share Matrix uses two simple metrics (relative market share and industry growth rate) and categorizes SBUs into four quadrants, which critics argue is overly simplistic compared to multi-factor matrices like GE or ADL.
Hard NORMAL · Forward Integration | Vertical Integration | Strategic Choices
A commercial airline company acquires a chain of hotels and tour operating agencies. This corporate growth strategy represents:
A. Backward Integration
B. Horizontal Integration
C. Concentric Diversification
D. Forward Vertical Integration ✔
Explanation: By acquiring tour operators and hotels, the airline moves downstream closer to the end customer's travel experience and service delivery, which constitutes forward vertical integration.
Hard NORMAL · BCG Matrix | Question Marks | Portfolio Analysis
Which of the following best characterizes the strategic intent of a 'Question Mark' in the BCG Matrix?
A. Milk for cash to fund other businesses.
B. Invest heavily to turn them into stars or divest if they consume resources without gaining share. ✔
C. Hold position and protect market share with minimal expenditure.
D. Liquidate immediately upon discovery.
Explanation: Question Marks (Problem Children) are high-growth, low-share businesses. They require high cash inputs to maintain or grow share, but their future is uncertain; management must decide whether to invest heavily to make them Stars or divest them.
Hard NORMAL · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | BCG Matrix | Portfolio Comparison
How does the GE Nine-Cell Matrix differ fundamentally from the BCG Growth-Share Matrix in terms of its axes?
A. GE uses subjective single-factor metrics, while BCG uses objective multi-factor metrics.
B. GE uses multi-factor composite dimensions (Industry Attractiveness and Business Strength), whereas BCG uses single-factor dimensions (Market Growth and Market Share). ✔
C. GE focuses only on international markets, while BCG focuses on domestic markets.
D. GE evaluates non-profit organizations, whereas BCG evaluates for-profit corporations.
Explanation: The key distinction is that BCG uses single-factor axes (relative market share and industry growth rate), whereas the GE matrix uses comprehensive, multi-factor composite indices for industry attractiveness and business strength.
Hard NORMAL · ADL Matrix | Divestment | Strategic Posture
In the ADL Matrix, what strategic posture is generally prescribed when an industry is in its mature or aging stage and the firm occupies a 'Weak' competitive position?
A. Fast growth and aggressive investment
B. Selective investment in niche areas
C. Harvesting or divestment / withdrawal ✔
D. Maintaining status quo
Explanation: In the ADL matrix, a firm with a weak competitive position in a mature or aging industry faces low future prospects and high vulnerability, making harvesting, turnaround, or divestment/withdrawal the appropriate strategic choice.
Hard NORMAL · Divestment | Spin-off | Retrenchment Strategies
A large pharmaceutical conglomerate spins off its agrochemical division into a completely separate legal entity with its own shares traded on the stock exchange. This is an example of:
A. Turnaround
B. Divestment via spin-off ✔
C. Liquidation
D. Backward Integration
Explanation: A spin-off is a form of divestment where a subsidiary or division is separated from the parent company to operate as an independent entity, allowing shareholders to hold shares in both firms directly.
Hard NORMAL · Differentiation | Competitive Advantage | Barriers to Imitation
When a firm pursues a differentiation strategy, which of the following isolating mechanisms or barriers protects its competitive advantage against imitators?
A. Pure reliance on low wages and low material costs
B. Patents, unique brand image, superior customer service, and complex product design ✔
C. Elimination of all R&D and marketing expenditures
D. Standardized mass production with zero customization
Explanation: Differentiation is protected by barriers such as brand loyalty, proprietary technology, patents, unique design features, and superior service quality, making it difficult and costly for competitors to duplicate.
Hard NORMAL · Combination Strategy | Grand Strategies | Strategic Choices
Which of the following scenarios best exemplifies a 'Combination Strategy' in corporate strategic management?
A. A firm adopts cost leadership in domestic markets and differentiation in international markets simultaneously or sequentially. ✔
B. A firm closes down all operations due to bankruptcy.
C. A firm merges with a direct competitor in the same market.
D. A firm focuses exclusively on a single product line in a single market.
Explanation: A combination strategy is adopted when an enterprise employs a mix of different grand strategies (such as stability for one division, expansion for another, and retrenchment for a third) simultaneously or sequentially across its business units.
CASE SCENARIO: Zenith Motors Ltd., an established automobile manufacturer in India, is reviewing its portfolio of business units and long-term growth options. The company operates four distinct units: Unit A (an electric scooter line in a high-growth emerging market with a dominant market share); Unit B (a legacy diesel hatchback model in a stagnant market with high market share); Unit C (an experimental flying-car prototype in a high-growth market with negligible market share); and Unit D (an outdated agricultural tractor division in a declining market with low market share). Zenith's board is evaluating how to allocate capital across these units using the BCG Growth-Share Matrix.
Medium SCENARIO · BCG Matrix | Stars | Portfolio Analysis
Based on the BCG Growth-Share Matrix, how should Unit A (electric scooter line with dominant share in a high-growth market) be classified?
A. Cash Cow
B. Star ✔
C. Question Mark
D. Dog
Explanation: Unit A operates in a high-growth market and holds a dominant market share, which places it squarely in the 'Star' category. Stars generate high incomes and require substantial investment to sustain their market leadership.
Medium SCENARIO · BCG Matrix | Cash Cows | Strategic Prescription
According to portfolio theory, what is the appropriate strategic treatment for Unit B (legacy diesel hatchback in a stagnant market with high market share)?
A. Inject massive fresh capital for aggressive expansion
B. Harvest and milk the unit for cash to fund other growing units ✔
C. Liquidate immediately without extracting any value
D. Classify as a Question Mark and increase marketing spend
Explanation: Unit B is a 'Cash Cow' (high share, low growth). The standard prescription is to milk it for cash with minimal reinvestment, using the surplus funds to support Stars and Question Marks.
Medium SCENARIO · BCG Matrix | Question Marks | Strategic Choice
How should Zenith categorize and manage Unit C (experimental flying-car in a high-growth market with negligible share)?
A. As a Dog; divest immediately
B. As a Cash Cow; use for dividend distribution
C. As a Question Mark; evaluate whether to invest heavily or divest ✔
D. As a Star; reduce prices to gain immediate share
Explanation: Unit C has low market share in a high-growth market, defining it as a Question Mark (or Problem Child). It requires careful analysis to decide if additional investment can turn it into a Star or if it should be abandoned.
Medium SCENARIO · BCG Matrix | Dogs | Divestment
What strategic decision does the BCG matrix typically recommend for Unit D (outdated tractor division in a declining market with low share)?
A. Divestment or liquidation ✔
B. Heavy investment to convert into a Star
C. Expansion into international markets
D. Conversion into a Cash Cow
Explanation: Unit D is a 'Dog' (low growth, low share). Dogs typically drain resources and offer poor profitability; the recommended strategy is divestment or liquidation.
CASE SCENARIO: Aura Cosmetics, a premium skincare brand known for its organic and chemical-free ingredients, is planning its growth trajectory for the next five years. The company currently sells its products exclusively through high-end specialty retail stores in major metropolitan cities in India. To achieve aggressive expansion, the management team is considering four distinct proposals: Proposal 1: Launching lower-priced herbal soaps in existing urban stores; Proposal 2: Entering the European and Southeast Asian retail markets with its existing product lineup; Proposal 3: Developing a new range of anti-aging serums containing patented botanical extracts for current urban customers; Proposal 4: Acquiring a chemical testing laboratory that previously served as Aura's key vendor.
Hard SCENARIO · Ansoff Matrix | Market Penetration | Growth Strategy
Proposal 1 (launching lower-priced herbal soaps in existing urban stores) represents which strategy under Ansoff's Product-Market Growth Matrix?
A. Market Development
B. Market Penetration ✔
C. Product Development
D. Diversification
Explanation: Launching new variations of products aimed at existing customer segments and stores falls under Market Penetration or Product Development depending on novelty, but introducing variations/extensions to capture more share in existing markets is primarily market penetration/expansion.
Medium SCENARIO · Ansoff Matrix | Market Development | Geographic Expansion
Proposal 2 (entering European and Southeast Asian retail markets with existing products) is an example of:
A. Market Development ✔
B. Product Development
C. Horizontal Integration
D. Backward Integration
Explanation: Taking existing products into new geographical markets is the classic definition of Market Development in Ansoff's Matrix.
Medium SCENARIO · Ansoff Matrix | Product Development | Strategic Choice
Proposal 3 (developing new anti-aging serums for current customers) corresponds to:
A. Market Penetration
B. Market Development
C. Product Development ✔
D. Conglomerate Diversification
Explanation: Product Development involves introducing new products to existing markets or customer segments, which matches developing anti-aging serums for current urban buyers.
Medium SCENARIO · Backward Integration | Vertical Integration | Corporate Strategy
Proposal 4 (acquiring the chemical testing laboratory that previously acted as a vendor) is an application of which corporate strategy?
A. Forward Integration
B. Backward Integration ✔
C. Horizontal Integration
D. Conglomerate Diversification
Explanation: Acquiring a supplier or vendor (testing lab) moves the firm upstream in the supply chain, which is Backward Integration.
CASE SCENARIO: Titanium Tech Solutions, a mid-sized IT hardware manufacturer, has been suffering from three consecutive years of heavy financial losses due to intense price wars initiated by low-cost Asian competitors, rising debt servicing costs, and bloated overheads. The board appoints a new CEO, seasoned in corporate turnarounds, to rescue the firm. The CEO's restructuring blueprint involves the following phases: Phase 1: Imposing an immediate hiring freeze, slashing administrative expenses by 35%, and selling off an idle manufacturing plant in Pune to clear immediate bank dues; Phase 2: Refocusing engineering efforts exclusively on high-margin enterprise servers rather than commoditized desktop PCs; Phase 3: Rebuilding customer trust through targeted quality guarantees and launching a revamped product line.
Medium SCENARIO · Turnaround Strategy | Retrenchment | Stabilization
Phase 1 of the restructuring blueprint (cost cutting, freezing hiring, and selling an idle plant) is characteristic of which stage in a Turnaround Strategy?
A. Recovery stage
B. Retrenchment/Stabilization stage ✔
C. Expansion stage
D. Liquidation stage
Explanation: The initial stage of a turnaround strategy is retrenchment/stabilization, which focuses on cutting costs, shedding non-performing assets, stopping cash bleed, and stabilizing the financial position.
Medium SCENARIO · Turnaround Strategy | Objectives | Retrenchment
What is the primary objective of Phase 1 in a turnaround situation?
A. To achieve global market leadership immediately
B. To stop the financial hemorrhage and stabilize operations ✔
C. To diversify into unrelated retail businesses
D. To merge with the lowest-cost competitor
Explanation: The primary objective of the retrenchment phase in a turnaround is to halt the financial losses and stabilize the firm's cash flows before embarking on recovery and growth.
Hard SCENARIO · Turnaround Strategy | Recovery Phase | Operational Restructuring
Phase 2 (refocusing on high-margin enterprise servers and abandoning commoditized PCs) represents which strategic action during a turnaround?
A. Asset reduction and downsizing
B. Core business refocusing and operational restructuring ✔
C. Total enterprise liquidation
D. Forward vertical integration
Explanation: After stabilization, the turnaround strategy moves to the recovery phase, which involves restructuring operations, focusing on core profitable segments (like enterprise servers), and shedding unprofitable product lines.
Medium SCENARIO · Liquidation Strategy | Retrenchment | Strategic Choices
If Titanium Tech Solutions fails to implement Phase 1 and Phase 2 successfully, and losses continue to mount with zero cash reserves, what is the ultimate recourse for the enterprise?
A. Market Development
B. Liquidation Strategy ✔
C. Diversification Strategy
D. Backward Integration
Explanation: When all turnaround and restructuring efforts fail to revive a loss-making enterprise, the final retrenchment alternative is Liquidation, involving the sale of all assets and closure of the business.
CASE SCENARIO: Nexus Pharma Corp. is evaluating its diverse portfolio of pharmaceutical and healthcare operations using the GE Nine-Cell Matrix. The board has analyzed two key SBU portfolios: SBU Alpha (specialized oncology drugs) and SBU Beta (over-the-counter standard pain relief tablets). SBU Alpha operates in an industry characterized by very high market growth, technological advancements, and strong profit margins, while Nexus Pharma holds a dominant market position and robust proprietary R&D capabilities in this segment. SBU Beta operates in a mature, highly competitive industry with slow growth, where Nexus Pharma faces moderate market share and intense price pressure from numerous generic manufacturers.
Medium SCENARIO · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | Industry Attractiveness | Business Strength
Based on the description of SBU Alpha (high industry attractiveness due to growth/margins and strong business strength due to R&D and market position), where would it fall on the GE Nine-Cell Matrix?
A. Low Attractiveness / Weak Strength
B. High Attractiveness / Strong Strength ✔
C. Medium Attractiveness / Average Strength
D. Low Attractiveness / Strong Strength
Explanation: SBU Alpha combines high industry attractiveness and strong business strength, placing it in the top-left cells of the GE matrix, which prescribes a strategy of investment and growth.
Medium SCENARIO · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | Investment Strategy | Growth
What is the strategic recommendation prescribed by the GE Matrix for an SBU located in the 'High Attractiveness / Strong Strength' zone?
A. Harvest or divest immediately
B. Invest / Grow aggressively ✔
C. Hold and preserve earnings without further investment
D. Liquidate assets
Explanation: For businesses in the strong/high quadrants of the GE Matrix, the recommended strategy is to invest and grow, capitalizing on market opportunities and building competitive advantage.
Hard SCENARIO · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | Positioning | Portfolio Analysis
Where would SBU Beta (mature slow-growth industry, moderate share, intense generic price pressure) likely be positioned on the GE Nine-Cell Matrix?
A. High Industry Attractiveness / Strong Business Strength
B. Medium-to-Low Industry Attractiveness / Average-to-Weak Business Strength ✔
C. High Industry Attractiveness / Weak Business Strength
D. Rapid Growth / Dominant Strength
Explanation: SBU Beta suffers from a mature slow-growth market (medium/low attractiveness) and moderate share under pressure (average/weak strength), placing it in the middle-to-lower cells requiring selective or hold/harvest strategies.
Hard SCENARIO · GE Nine-Cell Matrix | BCG Matrix Comparison | Portfolio Evaluation
How does the GE Nine-Cell Matrix improve upon the BCG Matrix in evaluating multi-business corporations like Nexus Pharma?
A. By using single-factor metrics that are easier to calculate.
B. By replacing market share and growth rate with multi-factor composite dimensions like industry attractiveness and business strength. ✔
C. By restricting analysis strictly to non-profit entities.
D. By eliminating the need for any subjective managerial judgment.
Explanation: The GE Nine-Cell Matrix is an enhancement over the BCG matrix because it replaces simplistic single-factor axes with rich, multi-factor composite dimensions (Industry Attractiveness and Business Strength), accommodating a wider range of strategic variables.
CASE SCENARIO: Omega Retail Corp., a nationwide supermarket chain, wants to solidify its market position against aggressive online e-commerce giants. The management is debating three distinct competitive approaches inspired by Michael Porter's Generic Strategies. Approach 1: Reengineering internal logistics, automating warehouses, and bulk-sourcing to achieve the absolute lowest operating cost in the retail sector, passing minor savings to price-sensitive masses. Approach 2: Establishing high-end gourmet experience stores with in-house artisanal bakeries, personal shopping assistants, and exclusive imported organic produce, charging premium prices. Approach 3: Ignoring nationwide operations and exclusively opening hyper-localized, ultra-convenient mini-stores in gated residential townships, stocking items precisely tailored to the dietary preferences of that specific community.
Medium SCENARIO · Porter Generic Strategies | Cost Leadership | Strategic Choices
Approach 1 (lowest operating cost, bulk-sourcing, serving price-sensitive masses) exemplifies which of Porter's Generic Strategies?
A. Differentiation
B. Cost Leadership ✔
C. Focus Strategy
D. Stuck in the Middle
Explanation: Achieving the lowest operating cost through scale, efficiency, and tight cost control to serve mass markets is the hallmark of the Cost Leadership strategy.
Medium SCENARIO · Porter Generic Strategies | Differentiation | Competitive Advantage
Approach 2 (gourmet experience stores, personal shoppers, premium pricing) represents which strategy?
A. Cost Leadership
B. Differentiation ✔
C. Cost Focus
D. Liquidation
Explanation: Offering unique store experiences, artisanal goods, and premium pricing is a classic implementation of a Differentiation strategy.
Medium SCENARIO · Porter Generic Strategies | Focus Strategy | Niche Marketing
Approach 3 (ultra-convenient mini-stores in gated communities with tailored stock) describes which generic strategy?
A. Broad Cost Leadership
B. Broad Differentiation
C. Focus Strategy ✔
D. Horizontal Integration
Explanation: Targeting a narrow, specific buyer segment (gated community residents) with tailored product offerings is a Focus strategy.
Hard SCENARIO · Porter Generic Strategies | Stuck in the Middle | Strategic Pitfalls
According to Michael Porter, what would happen to Omega Retail Corp. if it attempts to simultaneously provide the lowest prices in the country while offering expensive gourmet experiences and personal shoppers without committing to either?
A. It will achieve maximum profitability across all segments.
B. It will become 'Stuck in the Middle', resulting in inferior performance and eroded profitability. ✔
C. It will automatically attain monopoly status.
D. It will successfully execute a combination generic strategy.
Explanation: Porter explicitly warns that firms failing to make a clear choice between cost leadership and differentiation become 'Stuck in the Middle', which typically leads to poor strategic performance because the firm lacks the low cost for mass volume or the uniqueness for premium margins.

Paper 6: Financial Management and Strategic Management · Paper 6B · Chapter 5:

SM — 55 rows
Easy NORMAL · Strategy Implementation | Action Stage | Strategic Management
Which of the following best defines strategy implementation in the context of strategic management?
A. Formulating long-term vision and mission statements for the enterprise
B. The process of allocating financial resources exclusively to marketing departments
C. The action stage of strategic management where formulated strategies are translated into organizational action ✔
D. Evaluating the financial variance between projected and actual budgets annually
Explanation: Strategy implementation is often considered the action stage of strategic management. It involves translating formulated strategies, plans, and policies into day-to-day organizational activities and results across all levels of the enterprise.
Medium NORMAL · Formulation vs Implementation | Strategic Leadership | Management Process
How does strategy formulation fundamentally differ from strategy implementation?
A. Formulation focuses on efficiency, while implementation focuses on effectiveness
B. Formulation focuses on positioning forces before the action, whereas implementation manages forces during the action ✔
C. Formulation requires lower-level managers, while implementation is strictly for top management
D. Formulation is an ongoing operational process, while implementation is a one-time event
Explanation: Strategy formulation focuses on positioning forces before the action takes place, requiring intellectual rigor and analytical skills. Strategy implementation manages forces during the action, requiring strong leadership, motivational capabilities, and operational coordination.
Medium NORMAL · Organizational Structure | Divisional Structure | Implementation Framework
Which organizational structure type is characterized by a central executive office that coordinates and controls operations through divisional line managers?
A. Functional structure
B. Divisional structure ✔
C. Strategic Business Unit (SBU) structure
D. Matrix structure
Explanation: A divisional structure (by product, geography, or market) organizes activities into self-contained divisions where a central executive office oversees and coordinates operational performance through divisional heads.
Hard NORMAL · SBU Structure | Diversification | Structural Design
When an enterprise grows through unrelated diversification and has numerous distinct product-market segments, which structural arrangement is most appropriate to manage complexity?
A. Simple structure
B. Functional structure
C. Strategic Business Unit (SBU) structure ✔
D. Geographic matrix structure
Explanation: An SBU structure groups similar divisions into strategic business units, delegating authority and responsibility for each unit to a senior executive reporting directly to the chief executive. It is ideal for large firms with widely diverse products or markets.
Medium NORMAL · Matrix Structure | Dual Authority | Organizational Design
What is the primary disadvantage associated with a matrix organizational structure?
A. Complete lack of functional specialization
B. Dual lines of authority leading to potential confusion and conflict ✔
C. Excessive centralization of decision-making power at the top
D. Inability to handle project-based or temporary initiatives
Explanation: The matrix structure combines functional and product/project chains of command, resulting in dual lines of authority (two bosses). This complexity often creates employee confusion, turf wars, and high administrative overhead.
Easy NORMAL · Organizational Culture | Shared Values | Behavioral Norms
Which concept refers to the pattern of shared values, beliefs, and assumptions that shape organizational behavior and influence how work gets done?
A. Organizational design
B. Strategic control
C. Organizational culture ✔
D. Functional policy
Explanation: Organizational culture represents the shared values, beliefs, norms, and behavioral patterns that characterize an enterprise. A strong culture aligns employee behavior with strategic objectives and facilitates implementation.
Medium NORMAL · Strategic Leadership | Change Management | Implementation
What is the primary role of strategic leadership during the strategy implementation phase?
A. Preparing annual financial statements for statutory auditing
B. Managing the change process, inspiring personnel, and aligning capabilities with vision ✔
C. Conducting external macro-environmental scanning using PESTLE analysis
D. Setting up rigid bureaucratic controls to eliminate all operational discretion
Explanation: Strategic leadership involves guiding the organization through change, inspiring employees, overcoming resistance, and aligning organizational capabilities and culture with the newly formulated strategic direction.
Medium NORMAL · Balanced Scorecard | Strategic Control | Performance Measurement
Which tool or framework is commonly used to track financial and non-financial performance metrics across multiple organizational perspectives?
A. Balanced Scorecard ✔
B. BCG Matrix
C. GE Nine-Cell Matrix
D. Ansoff Product-Market Growth Matrix
Explanation: The Balanced Scorecard is a strategic performance management tool that measures organizational performance from four perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Processes, and Learning & Growth.
Medium NORMAL · Balanced Scorecard | Internal Processes | Operational Excellence
Which perspective of the Balanced Scorecard focuses on core competencies, cycle times, and operational excellence?
A. Financial perspective
B. Customer perspective
C. Internal business process perspective ✔
D. Learning and growth perspective
Explanation: The internal business process perspective evaluates how well the organization is running its key operations, focusing on quality, cycle time, productivity, and other process-oriented metrics that drive customer and financial success.
Medium NORMAL · Strategic Control | Monitoring | Environmental Shifts
What does strategic control primarily aim to accomplish?
A. Ensure that daily cash disbursements match petty cash vouchers
B. Monitor how well an enterprise responds to external environmental shifts and internal execution milestones ✔
C. Automatically penalize middle managers for quarterly sales shortfalls
D. Eliminate the need for operational budgeting and variance analysis
Explanation: Strategic control is designed to steer the organization through environmental shifts. It assesses whether the strategy is proceeding as planned and whether adjustments are needed due to unforeseen changes in internal or external conditions.
Easy NORMAL · Operational Control | Strategic Control | Performance Standards
Which of the following is an example of operational control rather than strategic control?
A. Evaluating whether a new international market entry strategy is viable
B. Monitoring daily manufacturing defect rates against established plant standards ✔
C. Assessing the long-term impact of disruptive technologies on industry structure
D. Reviewing overall corporate portfolio balance and capital allocation
Explanation: Operational control focuses on executing short-term actions and measuring performance against predetermined standards (such as daily scrap rates or inventory levels), whereas strategic control evaluates long-term strategic assumptions.
Easy NORMAL · Strategy Evaluation | Corrective Action | Performance Appraisal
What is meant by 'strategy evaluation' in the strategic management process?
A. The preliminary appraisal of macroeconomic trends before starting a business
B. The final appraisal of strategic results and the internal/external factors underlying them to take corrective action ✔
C. The statutory audit of annual accounts by an independent firm of chartered accountants
D. The psychological assessment of senior executives during succession planning
Explanation: Strategy evaluation involves appraising the effectiveness of executed strategies, examining the underlying assumptions, measuring organizational performance, and initiating corrective actions when deviations occur.
Hard NORMAL · Rumelt Evaluation Criteria | Consonance | Strategy Evaluation
According to Richard Rumelt, which criterion for evaluating strategies examines whether the strategy represents an adaptive response to the external environment and critical changes?
A. Consonance ✔
B. Advantage
C. Feasibility
D. Consistency
Explanation: Consonance refers to the need for strategies to represent an adaptive response to external environments and to the critical trends occurring within them. A strategy must match environmental threats and opportunities.
Hard NORMAL · Rumelt Criteria | Consistency | Goal Alignment
Under Rumelt's criteria, what does 'Consistency' mean in strategy evaluation?
A. The strategy must provide a sustainable competitive advantage over rivals
B. The strategy must not present mutually inconsistent goals and policies ✔
C. The strategy must be feasible within the physical and financial resource limits of the firm
D. The strategy must maintain continuous compliance with international labor laws
Explanation: Consistency requires that a strategy must not present mutually inconsistent goals and policies. Organizational sub-units and functional areas must pull in the same direction without conflicting mandates.
Hard NORMAL · Rumelt Criteria | Feasibility | Resource Allocation
Which of Rumelt's criteria assesses whether a strategy can be executed with the available financial, human, and physical resources of the organization?
A. Advantage
B. Consonance
C. Feasibility ✔
D. Consistency
Explanation: Feasibility tests whether a strategy can be attempted within the physical, human, and financial resources available to the enterprise. Overestimating resource capability leads to strategic failure.
Easy NORMAL · Milestones | Implementation Control | Progress Tracking
What is the primary purpose of establishing 'Milestones' during strategy implementation?
A. To delay decision-making until the final fiscal quarter ends ✔
B. To provide intermediate checkpoints for assessing progress and maintaining momentum
C. To serve as legal evidence in case of shareholder litigation
D. To calculate employee bonuses without relying on performance appraisals
Explanation: Milestones serve as intermediate targets or checkpoints during implementation, allowing management to track progress, ensure schedules are met, and take early corrective actions if slippage occurs.
Easy NORMAL · Functional Structure | Specialization | Organizational Design
Which structural form groups employees primarily by specialized skills and tasks, such as engineering, finance, marketing, and human resources?
A. Functional structure ✔
B. Divisional structure
C. Matrix structure
D. Network structure
Explanation: A functional structure organizes an enterprise around basic business functions like marketing, finance, production, and R&D, promoting operational specialization and centralized control.
Medium NORMAL · Organizational Culture | Resistance to Change | Cultural Barrier
What is a major risk when an organizational culture is rigidly entrenched and resistant to change during strategy implementation?
A. It speeds up execution by enforcing uniform obedience
B. It creates a barrier that blocks strategic realignment and adaptation ✔
C. It eliminates all agency costs within middle management
D. It guarantees high employee retention regardless of compensation
Explanation: While a strong culture aids implementation when aligned with strategy, a rigid or incompatible culture acts as a powerful barrier to change, often sabotaging new strategies that require different behaviors and values.
Medium NORMAL · Business Process Reengineering | Radical Redesign | Process Improvement
Which of the following best describes 'BPR' (Business Process Reengineering) in relation to strategy implementation?
A. Incremental cost-cutting on office supplies and travel budgets
B. Radical redesign of core business processes to achieve dramatic improvements in performance ✔
C. Outsourcing all accounting functions to a third-party service provider
D. Merging two distinct corporate cultures through mandatory workshops
Explanation: Business Process Reengineering (BPR) involves the fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes to achieve dramatic improvements in critical measures of performance such as cost, quality, service, and speed.
Medium NORMAL · Change Management | Lewin Model | Unfreezing
In the context of strategic change, what is 'unfreezing' according to Kurt Lewin's change model?
A. Freezing asset depreciation schedules during economic downturns
B. Breaking down the existing mindset and status quo to make the organization receptive to change ✔
C. Locking in new operational routines permanently
D. Restricting capital expenditures until strategy implementation is complete
Explanation: Unfreezing involves overcoming inertia and dismantling the existing mindset, habits, and status quo, thereby creating a psychological readiness and motivation in employees to accept new ways of operating.
Easy NORMAL · Change Management | Refreezing | Lewin Model
What is the final stage in Kurt Lewin's change process model?
A. Transitioning
B. Refreezing ✔
C. Evaluating
D. Reengineering
Explanation: KurtLewin's change model consists of three stages: Unfreezing, Changing (moving), and Refreezing. Refreezing institutionalizes the new behaviors, making them the standard operating procedure.
Easy NORMAL · Benchmarking | Best Practices | Performance Gaps
How does benchmarking contribute to effective strategy implementation?
A. It establishes arbitrary quotas that employees must meet under threat of termination
B. It compares an organization's processes and performance metrics against industry best practices to identify gaps ✔
C. It replaces the need for financial auditing by focusing exclusively on stock price
D. It automates routine manufacturing processes using artificial intelligence
Explanation: Benchmarking is the process of measuring an organization's internal processes and performance against best-in-class companies, helping management identify performance gaps and adopt superior practices.
Hard NORMAL · Holding Company Structure | Portfolio Control | Corporate Governance
What is the primary function of a holding company or conglomerate structure?
A. Directly managing day-to-day manufacturing operations across all subsidiaries
B. Holding equity in various autonomous companies while exercising financial and portfolio control ✔
C. Eliminating all functional departments at the corporate headquarters level
D. Standardizing product design across entirely unrelated industries
Explanation: A holding company structure involves a parent corporation that owns the voting stock of other companies (subsidiaries) but generally exercises broad financial and portfolio oversight rather than managing daily operations.
Hard NORMAL · Rumelt Criteria | Advantage | Competitive Position
Why is 'Advantage' considered a critical criterion in Richard Rumelt's strategy evaluation framework?
A. It checks if the firm can maintain a competitive advantage in resources, skills, or position ✔
B. It ensures that top executives receive maximum performance bonuses
C. It verifies that all marketing expenditures comply with statutory advertising codes
D. It guarantees zero financial leverage in the capital structure
Explanation: Advantage refers to the creation and maintenance of a superior competitive position. A strategy must provide either positional superiority, resource superiority, or skill superiority over competitors.
Hard NORMAL · Strategic Control | Strategic Surveillance | Environmental Monitoring
Which strategic control mechanism involves continuous monitoring of broad trends in the general environment that might invalidate strategic assumptions?
A. Special alert control
B. Premise control
C. Implementation control
D. Strategic surveillance ✔
Explanation: Strategic surveillance is a broad-based, generalized monitoring tool that tracks a wide range of events inside and outside the organization that might threaten the current strategy.
Hard NORMAL · Premise Control | Strategic Assumptions | Control Techniques
What is the purpose of 'Premise Control' as a strategic control technique?
A. Checking whether physical security premises and warehouses are guarded against theft
B. Verifying and monitoring the key assumptions and premises upon which a strategy was built ✔
C. Inspecting manufacturing factory premises before granting operating licenses
D. Auditing preliminary project feasibility reports prepared by consultants
Explanation: Premise control is designed to check regularly whether the key assumptions and planning premises (such as economic growth rates, regulatory changes, inflation) underlying the strategy remain valid.
Medium NORMAL · Special Alert Control | Crisis Management | Trigger Events
When is a 'Special Alert Control' triggered in strategic management?
A. At the end of every fiscal quarter during routine board meetings
B. When an unexpected, high-impact event (such as a natural disaster or sudden regulatory ban) occurs ✔
C. Whenever employee attendance drops below ninety percent
D. During annual performance appraisals of entry-level staff
Explanation: Special alert control is triggered by sudden, unexpected events—such as major geopolitical crises, natural disasters, or competitor breakthroughs—that demand immediate reassessment of the strategy.
Medium NORMAL · Balanced Scorecard | Learning and Growth | Intangible Assets
What does the 'Learning and Growth' perspective in the Balanced Scorecard primarily measure?
A. Return on capital employed and net profit margins
B. Employee training, corporate culture, technological capabilities, and organizational climate ✔
C. Customer satisfaction scores and market share percentage
D. Speed of order delivery and manufacturing defect rates
Explanation: The learning and growth perspective focuses on the organization's intangible assets, particularly its people, culture, training, and technology infrastructure, which form the foundation for long-term success.
Hard NORMAL · Functional Structure | Growth Limitations | Organizational Evolution
How does a functional structure typically react as an enterprise grows and diversifies its product lines?
A. It becomes increasingly efficient and requires no structural modifications
B. It suffers from coordination bottlenecks, functional silos, and overloaded top management ✔
C. It automatically transforms into a matrix structure without executive intervention
D. It eliminates the need for middle management entirely
Explanation: As a firm grows and diversifies, the functional structure leads to coordination problems, communication barriers between departments (silos), and excessive burdens on top management, necessitating a shift to divisional or SBU structures.
Medium NORMAL · Cultural Audit | Strategy Implementation | Organizational Culture
What is the primary focus of corporate culture audit during strategy implementation?
A. Auditing petty cash receipts and employee travel expenses
B. Assessing whether existing cultural values and norms support or hinder the new strategic direction ✔
C. Counting the number of cultural events hosted by the HR department
D. Measuring physical office space allocation among senior executives
Explanation: A cultural audit examines the prevailing values, beliefs, and behavioral norms of the organization to determine compatibility with the new strategy, enabling management to address cultural resistance proactively.
CASE SCENARIO: Zenith Motors Ltd., an established automobile manufacturer in India, formulated a bold new strategy to transition entirely from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs) over a three-year period. Furthermore, middle managers resisted the shift, citing unfamiliarity with EV technology and clinging to legacy manufacturing processes. To monitor this complex transformation, Rajesh decided to implement a Balanced Scorecard alongside continuous milestone tracking.

C. Adopting a holding company structure with zero operational oversight

Medium SCENARIO · Balanced Scorecard | Learning and Growth | Skill Enhancement
If Zenith Motors uses the Balanced Scorecard, which perspective would specifically track employee training hours on EV battery technology and internal skill enhancement?

Explanation: The learning and growth perspective focuses on organizational capital, including employee training, skill development, corporate culture, and technology readiness.
Medium SCENARIO · Milestones | Implementation Control | Progress Tracking
When Rajesh Sharma tracks intermediate targets such as prototype completion dates and pilot testing schedules, what implementation tool is he utilizing?
A. Milestones ✔

CASE SCENARIO: Aura Pharmaceuticals, a mid-sized drug manufacturer, recently acquired two smaller biotech firms specializing in generic oncology drugs. A. It forces all three diverse sectors to share a single centralized manufacturing plant
B. It groups similar divisions into distinct strategic business units, enabling focused management of diverse product-market segments ✔
C. It eliminates the need for any corporate headquarters oversight
D. It replaces divisional managers with functional supervisors
Explanation: An SBU structure groups similar divisions into strategic business units, allowing large firms with diverse operations to manage distinct product-market segments effectively under senior executive leadership.
Hard SCENARIO · Rumelt Criteria | Consistency | Goal Alignment
Which of Rumelt's evaluation criteria addresses the board's concern regarding whether the farm mechanization SBU's expansion strategy conflicts with the corporate cash conservation mandate?
A. Consistency ✔
B. Advantage
C. Consonance
D. Feasibility
Explanation: Consistency evaluates whether organizational goals and functional policies are mutually compatible, ensuring that an SBU's strategy does not contradict corporate-level financial mandates.
Hard SCENARIO · Strategic Surveillance | Environmental Scanning | Control Techniques
Which control mechanism would AgroCorp's board use to continuously scan broad macroeconomic and agricultural policy trends (such as changes in government fertilizer subsidies) that could impact all SBUs?
A. Strategic surveillance ✔
B. Special alert control
C. Plant scrap control
D. Invoice verification control
Explanation: Strategic surveillance is a generalized, broad-based monitoring mechanism designed to track macroeconomic, regulatory, and industry trends across the general environment.
Hard SCENARIO · Rumelt Criteria | Consonance | Environmental Adaptation
When evaluating strategy, what does 'Consonance' specifically require AgroCorp to assess?
A. Whether the corporate office has enough petty cash for office supplies
B. Whether each SBU's strategy represents an adaptive response to external environmental changes and industry trends ✔
C. Whether all employees have identical job titles across divisions
D. Whether software licenses are renewed annually
Explanation: Consonance requires that a strategy represent an adaptive response to the external environment and the critical trends occurring within it.
